Ministry are still awaited.  
 Para: 17, 19, 23, 42, 44, 45, 58, 59, 62, 65 and 83 (Total: 11) 
 
 
3. The details of the Action Taken Replies of the Ministry and fu rther 
recommendations/observations of the Committee thereon wherever found necessary are given in 
the succeeding pages. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 2 
 
CHAPTER – I 
 
THE RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS, WHICH HAVE BEEN 
ACCEPTED BY THE MINISTRY 
   
Recommendation/ Observation 
1. The Automobile Sector, due to its strong forward and backward linkages with 
several key segments of   the economy, occupies   a  prominent  place in   the fabric of 
Indian Economy. Since the number of vehicles exported in various segments is nowhere 
near the potential, exporting vehicles in a large scale would significantly contribute to 
employment generation, trade balance and economic growth of the country. The 
Committee therefore recommends that constructive steps should be taken by the 
Government to pro mote export of vehicles in various segments, particularly the BS -VI 
compliant vehicles, and their engine & spare parts to various countries across the globe, 
especially to Africa, Latin America, Southeast Asia and West Asia where there is still 
huge potential for the global automobile companies operating from India. The Committee 
also recommends that the Government in coordination with the automobile companies 
should take appropriate steps   to explore the rural markets, particularly in Two Wheeler 
and Three  Wheeler segments that would contribute substantially for the growth of the 
Auto Sector. 
        (Para 30) 
Action Taken Replies 
 With regards to providing support to auto industry for enhancing exports , the 
following steps have been taken in this direction. 
i)          PLI scheme for the auto sector has been notified with an outlay of Rs 25,938 
crore to enhance the competitiveness of the industry and will help it attain higher 
foothold in exports.  
A number of schemes such as Mahatma Gandhi National Rural E mployment 
Guarantee Act (MNREGA), PradhanMantri Gram SadakYojana (PMGSY), and National 
Social Assistance Programme (NSAP) have been launched for the development of rural 
markets.  It is imperative to recognise that infrastructure is a major driver of growt h for 
auto industry. Consistent allocation of enhanced budget greatly emphasised on the rural 
population, the underprivileged, infrastructure development and development of National 
Highways is significant to give boost to economy especially  with 
focus on rural infrastructure creating a robust business environment an d thus, helping 
auto industry to contribute positively towards National GDP.  
The Two wheeler companies (2W) have already traced the r ural sector, becoming 
the major contributor of automobile sales in this area, Apart from OEMs, Federation of 
Automobile Dealers‟ Association(FADA) may increase their rural penetration  and 
Automotive Skill Development Council need to made rural people   aware of the job 

 3 
opportunities that they might land into after training and show them the path from skill to 
entrepreneurship. 
In a way, COVID-19 has  also contributed in growth of automobile in rural areas as the 
migrants who have gone back duringCOVID-19 to their native villages require an 
alternative source of income enabling pickups, 3-wheelers and LCVs to sell faster in rural 
markets. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
2. The Committee is of the view that in addition to setting of Automotive Vehicle 
Scrapping Facility (AVSF) centres across the country, the government sho uld make 
provisions for upfront financial incentives in the Scrappage Policy to boost demand for 
purchase of new vehicles. The proposed financial incentives would encourage end users 
to discard their old and polluting vehicles and go in for purchase of the  new BS VI 
compliant vehicles.                (Para 68)                                                                                                                       
 
3. Further, the Committee also recommends that adequate transparency should be 
maintained while selecting the proposed AVSF centre, which should be based on 
adherence to pre decided parameters that have to be met by such centres. 
        (Para 69) 
Action Taken Replies For Para 3 & 4 
MoRT&H has undertaken following initiatives to phase out old and unfit vehicles:-  
1.Draft GSR Notification 190(E )dt 15.03.2021 -The Draft Notification provides Motor 
Vehicles (Registration and Functions of Vehicle Scrapping Facility) Rules, 2021 for 
establishment of Registered Vehicles Scrapping Facility (RVSF) to ensure transparency in 
the selection of RVSF.  
2.Draft GSR Notification 177(E) dt 12.03.2021 - The Draft Notification provides that 
Certificate of Registration of Government -owned Vehicles would be non -renewable on 
lapse of 15 years.  
3.Draft GSR N otification 191 (E) dt 15.03.2021 - The Draft Notification provides for 
revision of registration fee, fitness testing fee and fitness certification fee of vehicles. The 
initiative is towards creation of an ecosystem for phasing out of older polluting vehicles.  
4.Draft GSR Notification 220 (E) dt26.03.2021 - The Draft Notification provides for 
concession in the motor vehicle tax for the vehicle registered against submission of 
"Certificate of vehicle scrapping".  
5.Draft GSR Notification 278(E ) dt 08.04.2021 - The Draft Notification provides for 
recognition, regulation and control of Automated Testing Stations.  
All the above initiatives are to ensure transparency in the vehicle scrapping process. 
 
 

 4 
Recommendation/ Observation 
4. The Committee notes that the core objective of Automotive Mission Plan (2026) is 
to propel the Indian Automobile Industry to be the engine of the "Make in  India" 
Programme as it is among the foremost drivers of the manufacturing  sector. In this 
regard, the Committee was informed by the  Federation  of  Automobile Dealers 
Association that if Foreign Direct Investment is allowed in auto sector, it will allow 
Indian Auto Dealers to expand by attracting foreign investment and collaborate with 
dealership groups internationally, without compro mising their ownership. FADA also 
stressed the need to have a Franchise Act for Auto Dealers specifically in our country, on 
the lines of other countries in the world. The Committee, therefore, recommends the 
aforesaid suggestions made by the FADA. 
        (Para 71) 
Action Taken Replies 
 The Government of India encourages foreign investment in the automobile sector 
and has allowed 100% foreign direct investment (FDI) under the automatic route except 
Note 3 of FDI Policy wherein GOI mandates that FDI would b e allowed from all 
neighbouring countries to India (with whom India shares a land border) only after 
obtaining approval of the GOI, even in sectors where “automatic” clearances were 
previously permitted.   
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
5. Given the characte ristic of the Covid -19 pandemic world over, the Committee 
understands that this disease is expected to exist for more time. The Committee 
appreciates the Government's decision of graded opening of the lockdown and restarting 
the economic activity for life to  move-on  along with  the Corona virus side by side. The 
Committee however recommends that with a view to protect life and livelihood, the 
economy  needs  to  be opened  up gradually  ensuring : the   safety  to life.    Therefore, 
the Committee, with re gard to Automobile Se ctor, recommends that the Government 
should issue guidelines and Standard Operational Procedures (SOP) that all the 
concerned stakeholders should prioritize employee protection and safety, regularly 
monitor and track health status of t he employees, follow disease control protocols, define 
travel guidelines, ensure quarantine facility, schedule for flexible working hours etc. 
        (Para 80) 
Action Taken Replies 
 Various government & autonomous bodies strictly followed the guidelines a nd 
Standard Operating Procedures (SOP) issued by Ministry of Home Affairs and Ministry 
of Health & Family Welfare  to ensure safety of employees for resuming work post 
COVID-19 lockdown.  Various employee and customers‟ safety control measures were 
being taken. Some of them are as following:- 
 Social distancing at workplace 
 Sanitization of vehicles & premises, status of Aarogya Setu App 
 Mandatory wearing of face mask, contribution to PM care relief fund, working in 
shifts to ensure social distancing 

 5 
 Invested in safety initiatives, procurements of sanitizers, thermal scanners, 
oximeters etc. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
6. The Committee notes the recent announcement of relief package by the 
Government to reboot the economy to tide over the crisis and extend supp ort to the 
various stakeholders, like infusion of liquidity through Collateral Free Automatic Loans, 
Subordinate Debt Scheme, financial support to NBFCs etc. which will encourage new 
investments, promoting growth across the supply chain, including Automobi le Dealers, 
and safeguarding employment. Although the package has infused a fresh lease of life 
amid the gloom, but at the same time, the Committee however feels that this stimulus 
package in particularly, falls short of addressing the issues of the Automo tive Industry as 
the measures taken by the Government is targeted to boost only the supply side of the 
economy. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the government should focus on 
announcing a stimulus package  for demand generation for the automotive sector where 
the government spending could boost a faster revival of the economy. 
        (Para 81) 
Action Taken Replies 
In line with the clarion call of Hon‟ble Prime Minister towards AtmaNirbhar 
Bharat, the Union Cabinet has recently, given its approval to introduce the Production-
Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme worth up to INR 1.45 lakh crore in 10 key sectors t o 
 enhance India‟s Manufacturing Capabilities and Exports including PLI for Automobiles.   
Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Automobile and Auto Components 
Industry in India has been approved by Union Cabinet on 15.09.2021. Incentives worth Rs 
25938 crore will be provided to industry over period of five years  
i.e from FY 2022 -23 to FY 2026 -27. The Scheme and its Guidelines have been Notifi ed 
on 23.09.2021. 
 This Production Linked Incentive (PLI) Scheme for Automobile and Auto components 
proposes financial incentives to boost domestic manufacturing of  
Advanced Automotive Technology products and attract investments in the automotive 
manufacturing value chain. Its prime objectives include overcoming cost disabilities, 
creating economies of scale and building a robust supply chain in areas of Advanced 
Automotive Technology products. It will also generate employment. This scheme will 
facilitate the Automobile Industry to move up the value chain into higher value added 
products. 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
7. Further, to attract the foreign Companies to set shop pertaining to the Automotive 
Sector in the Indian soil , the prevalent land and labour  laws of the country may need an 
overhauling, so as to make it more investor friendly. The Committee,   accordingly,  
recommends  that  DHI  may  take  up  the issue  with  the appropriate Departments of 
the Government of India to facilitate the same. 
        (Para 86) 
 

 6 
Action Taken Replies 
 Ministry of Labour has intimated that the Government has notified four Labour 
Codes; namely, the Code on Wages, 2019, the Industrial Relations Code 2020, the Code 
on Social Security, 2020 and the Occupational Safety, Hea lth and Working Conditions 
Code, 2020 by simplifying, amalgamating and rationalizing the relevant provisions of 
Central Labour Laws.   Codification of the Labour laws will inter alia reduce 
multiplication of definitions & authorities facilitating implementa tion & use of 
technology in enforcement of labour laws and bring transparency,  , accountability in 
enforcement thereby promoting setting up of more enterprises.  Further, provisions of one

with the direction to ensure the implementation of the guidelines. It may be noted that the 
Ministry of Road Transport and Highways is the nodal ministry in this mat ter and 
MoEF&CC  provides support from time to time.              (Para 77) 
 
Further Recommendation/Observation for Para 49, 50, 51, 52 and 77 
The Committee notes from the written submission from the Ministry that the  
Compensation Cess on Internal Combustion Engine (ICE) vehicles are levied not on 
a fixed slab and it is based on the size of the engine of the vehicle in Cubic Capacity 
(CC). Therefore, the Committee reiterates that GST rates on ICE vehicles should 
also be levied on the basis of their sizes  i.e  CC rather than having a fixed slab on all 
categories which is currently taxed at the top slab of 28%  without any distinction of 
small, mid and luxury vehicles.  The Committee feels that the small and mid 
segment vehicles should be taxed at a comparative ly lower slab than the luxury 
vehicles in order to make small and mid vehicles more affordable which in turn 
create demand and boost sales.  The Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) being the 
nodal agency for drafting p olicies for the Auto Industry  should pursue this matter 
with the GST Council and also bring the observations of the Committee to the notice 
of GST Council. 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 

 21 
CHAPTER – IV 
RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS IN RESPECT OF WHICH THE 
FINAL REPLIES OF THE MINISTRY ARE STILL AWAITED 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
28. The Committee was informed by the Auto Industry Associations that the non  
availability of finance to consumers due to tightening of norms for retail financing by the 
Banks across the board in rural as well as urban areas has a ffected the growth of the 
Auto Industry Sector. This approach by banks has reduced the availability of finance to 
customers to go in for new vehicle purchase. Further, Banks are following CIBIL ratings 
in a very rigorous manner as a result of which the cus tomers are finding it difficult to get 
automobile loans. Most of the two wheeler customers are first time users and they don't 
have any CIBIL ratings or credit ratings. Moreover, the markets are shifting towards 
rural markets, where potential customers fin d in difficult for getting loans as they do not 
have any record of financial security, since they do not pay income tax. So with 
increasing stringent compliance measures, the rural customers find it difficult to avail 
finance from the banks for purchasing new vehicles. Earlier financing of about 85 -90 
percent was available but now it is limited to only 60 -70%. As per the submission 9f 
Department of Heavy Industry, amongst all the sectoral loans, NPAs are the least at 1.5 - 
2% for Auto Loans. The Committee n otes that majority of vehicle purchases are made 
through loans. The Auto loan is a secured loan as the vehicle itself is collateral. The 
Committee, therefore, finds no reason why the banks should be refusing auto loans to 
prospective consumers. The Committ ee, therefore, recommends that Department of 
Heavy Industry should take up the matter with Department of Financial Services for 
issuing required instructions to all banks throughout the country to adopt a liberal policy 
in sanctioning of vehicle loans subj ect to minimum regulations of fulfilling the eligibility 
condition. 
       (Para 17) 
Action Taken Replies 
Matter has been taken up with Department of Financial Services for their favourable 
consideration of the matter. 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
29. The Ministry of Finance in their written submission has stated that funds worth 
Rs.70,000 crore have been released for PSU banks recapitalization to improve liquidity 
situation. The Committee is pleased to note the action taken by the Government to 
strengthen the bank liquidity and believes that such a move will help PSU Banks to boost 
lending and improve liquidity situation. Further, the NBFCs  will be allowed to use 
Aadhar authenticated KYCs to take up credit which would further help them to lend more 
Auto Loans. The Committee hopes that this move  by the Ministry of Finance would bring 
some respite to the Auto buyers   in the  country and help improve the downturn in the 
Automobile Sector.        
        (Para 19) 
 
 

 22 
Action Taken Replies 
Matter has been taken up  with Department of Financial Services for their favourable 
consideration of the matter. 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
30. The Committee is therefore of the considered opinion that  as  far  as  the working 
capital requirement of Auto Dealers is   concerned,  collateral  norms  for regular loan 
products should be moderate for availing   required finance.   The Committee is of the 
view that though banks have been facing various   challenges because of bad loans, 
however, they should not look at all financial lend ings with the same eye as the recovery 
rate is very high in the auto sector. Therefore, all measures needs to be taken to ease the 
availability of finance to the stakeholders in order to help them contribute substantially 
for the revival of auto sector. 
        (Para 23) 
Action Taken Replies 
 
Matter has been taken up with Department of Financial Services for their favourable 
consideration of the matter. 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
31. The Committee notes that the over impetus and aggressive targeting by th e 
Government on EV and its high  cost price, have created  confusion  in the  minds  of the  
consumer whether to go in for   purchase of EV or ICE   vehicle, who were already in the 
wait and watch mode in the wake of mandated transition from BS -IV to BS  VI w.e.f. 1st 
April, 2020. The Committee recommends that the MoRTH should comeout with clear 
picture on the future of ICE technology and adoption of Electric Mobility for a 
synergised co-existence. 
        (Para 42) 
Action Taken Replies 
The matter is under ac tive consideration with Ministry of Road Transport and 
Highways. 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
32. The Committee is of the view that the Government should conduct a thorough 
study and incorporate necessary provision for eco -friendly management/disposal of u sed 
LIBs so that E-waste does not turn out to be environment hazard. 
        (Para 44) 
Action Taken Replies 
The Draft Batteries Waste Management Rules were notified in February 2020. The Rules 
will deal with the environmentally sound management of all type s of batteries including 
lithium-ion batteries 

 23 
Recommendation/ Observation 
33. The Committee also recommends that DHI should take initiatives to foray into 
new and emerging technological areas instead of concentrating solely on the expensive 
lithium ion ba sed battery operated electric vehicles. The Committee feels that other 
avenues such as hydrogen based fuel cell technology etc. may be tapped and explored. By 
adopting such multi -pronged approach, the Committee is of the opinion that the EV 
industry would not be constrained to depend on its survival solely on the imported lithium 
based ion cell battery. 
        (Para 45) 
Action Taken Replies 
To promote New/Clean Technology  & Vehicle fuel, Ministry of New and Renewable 
Energy has drafted a National Hydrogen Energy Mission document which would inter-alia 
aim to scale up Green Hydrogen production and utilization across multiple sectors, 
including transportation. The Ministry has taken a pilot project for the said purpose. 
Recommendation/ Observation 
34. The Committee feels that the Government should work out a feasible measure to 
help these customers to own new Two Wheelers which would also help revival of the Auto 
industry.  Further the Committee, recommends that the Government should gear up the 
implementation mechanism to ensure that there is no defaulting in Insurance Renewal by 
the Vehicle Owners. 
        (Para 58) 
Action Taken Replies 
Matter has been taken up with Department of Financial Services for their favourable 
consideration of the matter 
Recommendation/ Observation 
35. Further, to offset the  burden  on the consumer  due to hike in the  amount as well 
as number of years of Insurance coverage, the Committee   recommends  that facility for  
provision of loan to meet the cost of Insurance coverage   be ma de,  by taking up the 
matter with the appropriate authorities by the DHI. 
        (Para 59) 
Action Taken Replies 
The matter is under consultation with Ministry of Finance and Ministry of Road 
Transport & Highways. 
 
 
 
 
 

 24 
Recommendation/ Observation 
36. The  Committee notes that the present system of transferring of vehicles from one 
state to other states is time consuming and cumbersome   because  it  involves manual 
interaction with   State Transport Authorities. Taking cue   from   this situation, the 
Committee in  its recent Report   on  the  Demands for   Grants (2020-21), in respect of 
DHI, which was presented to the House on 3rd March 2020, had recommended   for a  
uniform  Road Tax across all States. The Committee is   hopeful that Government will be 
able to get through the proposal  in  the  Transport Development Council for introducing 
One Nation-One Tax for benefit of the people. 
        (Para 62) 
Action Taken Replies 
 A Group of Transport Ministers of States (GOM) was constituted during the 38 th 
meeting of the Transport Development Council (TDC) held on 19.09.2017 at Vadodara, 
Gujarat. The first   meeting of GOM was held on 19.06.2018 at Guwahati and the GOM 
took cognizance of this matter of „One Nation -One Tax‟. The group was of the 
unanimous opinion that t he diverse road tax structure for motor vehicles was a major 
reason behind this long pending issue. There is an urgent need to harmonize the rates of 
road tax across the states. The group made several recommendations for implementation 
of the concept of on e-nation-one road tax. Accordingly, a concept paper has been 
prepared by MORT&H and has been shared with States for their views on the paper.  
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
37. The Committee is of the opinion that the decision of the Government to increase 
the depreciation rate for vehicles is a short term measure and therefore, recommends that 
the Government may consider introducing an effective depreciation rate as 25%, (Written 
Down Value) on a permanent  basis to have depreciation value equal to real useful life of 
the vehicles. 
        (Para 65) 
Action Taken Replies 
 Matter has been taken up with Department of Financial Services for their 
favourable consideration of the matter. 
 
Recommendation/ Observation 
38. Since the physical distancing is one of the pre-requisites to tackle the corona 
virus spread, it is expected that a large number of people would switch over to personal 
mobility from public transport to commute for safety reasons to avoid jostling with others 
on crowded buses and trains. As most of these people would be first time buyers, the 
Committee expects an immediate surge in the purchase of affordable two -wheeler or 
small and mid -sized cars. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Government 
should capitalize this trend for promoting sale  of small and midsize cars by ensuring 

 25 
availability of finance through easy vehicle loans at low interest rates to the prospective 
customers to create demand in the Automobile Sector. 
        (Para 83) 
 
Action Taken Replies 
 Matter has been taken up with D epartment of Financial Services for their 
favourable consideration of the matter.

Recommendation/Observation 
1.  The Committee takes note of the data furnished by DPE regarding production by 
CPSEs and recognizes the severity of operational disruptions i n CPSEs due to complete 
lockdown. The Committee, therefore, is of the opinion that a detailed study needs to be 
conducted to comprehend at micro -level; the actual impact of COVID -19 Pandemic and 
consequent lockdowns on the performance of the CPSEs so that necessary timely 
intervention by the Government can be made to mitigate the economic fallout.  
(Para 10) 
 Action Taken Replies 
 The Department of Public Enterprises (DPE) has informed that they collect 
information on performance  relating to all the CPSEs a nnually and brings out  a 
comprehensive Public Enterprises Survey which is laid on the table of  both the House of 
the Parliament. The recommendation of the Hon‟ble Committee would be duly 
considered while preparing the Public Enterprises Survey for the year  2020-21 to include 
a chapter on impact of COVID -19 pandemic and consequent lockdowns on the 
performance of CPSEs. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
2.  The Committee notes that BHEL in collaboration with NTPC & IGCAR, with 
funding support from DHI is developing  Advanced Ultra Super Critical Technology for 
thermal power generation, which is an indigenous technology being developed for the 
first time in India. Since the R&D phase of the said project is in the final stages, as 
informed by DHI, the Committee is of t he view that initiatives may be taken for exploring 
the domestic power market using the new technology to supplement the Make in India 
initiative. 
(Para 35.14) 
Action Taken Replies 
All the envisaged seven (07) major technical milestones pertaining to the “ R&D 
Project for Development of Advanced Ultra Super -critical (AUSC) Technology for 
Thermal Power Plants” (Phase-1) were completed / achieved by December 2020, and the 
financial closure of R&D Phase-1 was accomplished in March 2021. 
  The next intended footstep, i.e. Phase-2, involves setting up of a 1x800 MW coal -
fired AUSC technology demonstration plant (TDP) under the aegis of Ministry of Power 
(MoP). In this regard, NTPC Ltd. and BHEL have signed a MoU (Memorandum of 
Understanding) in July 2019 for forma tion of Joint Venture (JV) company for setting up 

 3 
of 1x800 MW AUSC TDP at Sipat site of NTPC Ltd. The approval for Phase -2, which 
encompasses financial support from Government of India, is under purview of NTPC 
Ltd. and Ministry of Power. The technical spe cifications of the TDP are under process of 
finalisation. Further steps shall be taken after the successful implementation of the AUSC 
technology in the TDP. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
3.  The Committee notes that 40% of the component required for HMT Machines viz. 
CNC Controllers & Drivers, Spindle Bearings, Linear Motion Guides etc were imported. 
However, disruptions in import due to lockdowns and closure of ports have 
adversely affected the productions. Efforts have been made by HMT to provide technical  
support to Domestic Manufactures and utilize its infrastructure facilities for production 
of import substitutions. The Committee observes that the turnover and profit/loss for the 
2nd quarter have been poorer than that of 1st quarter of the current FY 202 0-21. The 
Committee recommends that new avenues may be explored for alternate manufacturing 
hubs for import substitution and technology transfer from other countries to meet the 
requirements of HMT so that the production process is back on track. 
(Para 41.10) 
Action Taken Replies 
HMT Limited has been looking for alternate sources and is encouraging domestic 
manufactures to take up manufacturing of the items which were hitherto imported. With 
the easing of disruptions due to lockdown and opening of ports, th e production process 
has been on track in the third and fourth quarters of financial year 2020-21. 
 
Recommendation/Observation 
4.         The Committee recommends that DHI should make concerted efforts to uplift the 
company from its dependency on Chinese r aw materials and co -ordinate with concerned 
Indian stakeholders, who would be able to provide the Company with the requisite raw -
materials, so as to facilitate the Company to realise the vision of an ‘Atmanirbhar 
Bharat’. 
     (Para 43.10) 
Action Taken Replies 
REIL has partially arranged few items such as solar cell from other sources which 
were procured from China. However, continuous efforts are being made for procurement 
of other components/items such as semiconductors, thermal printer, LCD etc.  from 
indigenous sources /  other countries, which may result into positive output in terms of 
having independency from Chinese market and the initiatives taken by the Company will 
provide impetus in achieving its goal of „Atmanibhar Bharat‟. 
 

 4 
Recommendation/Observation 
5. The Committee observes that under the Public Procurement Policy (PPP), the 
MSEs are promoted to improve their market accessibility and competitiveness through 
increased participation in Government procurements and encouraging development of 
linkages between MSEs and PSEs. As per the mandate of the Public Procurement Policy 
for Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs) Order 2012, every Central Ministries/PSEs 
should set an annual target of minimum 25% procurement of goods & services from MSE 
Sector. Out of 25% annual procurement, a sub -target of 4% & 3% should be from MSEs 
owned by SC/ST and Women entrepreneurs, respectively. Keeping in view the 
extraordinary situation, the Committee is of the view that the Central Ministries and 
PSUs may procure more than  the prescribed limits laid down under the PPP for MSES 
Order 2012, so as to give further boost to the localized production. 
 (Para 56)   
Action Taken Replies 
Ministry of Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises has informed that they have 
taken various initiativ es to improve the market accessibility and competitiveness of 
MSEs through increased participation in Government procurement and encouraging 
development of linkages between MSEs and CPSEs. In FY 2020 -21, 141 CPSEs had 
procured Rs.39,557.34 crore (31.69%) o f goods and services from MSEs (including 
SCs/STs), which is more than the mandated target 25%. Furthermore, the 
recommendation of the Committee has been forwarded to all the Ministries/Departments 
and also to CPSEs by DPE to take note of it for consideration and compliance. 
Recommendations rece ived from the Committee has been conveyed to CPSEs for 
compliance.  
Recommendation/Observation 
6. The Committee takes note of the new initiative taken by DHI for constitution of 
Project Development Cell (PDC) for attracting investments and development of investible 
projects in India in coordination with various other Ministries/Departments and State 
Governments. The Committee desires that the details of the roadmap formulated by PDC 
for providing support to investors for investing in India in the automobile and auto 
components sector, capital goods sector etc. may be furnished for information of the 
Committee.  
(Para 58.1.2) 
Action Taken Replies 
Project Development Cell (PDC) was constituted and operationalized in  June 
2020 in this Ministry . Strategy to attract investments fall under the following 4 
categories: 
 

 5 
 One-to-one investor engagement: 
  MHI has been interacting with multiple individual investors in the automotive, 
auto components, electric mobility and capital  goods sectors. The purpose of these calls 
is to understand and facilitate the India investment plans of companies, through extension 
of support at the Central and State Government level. 
 Investment focused webinars: 
  In the post -COVID19 era, virtual inv estment-focused webinars are the primary 
means of reaching a wider investor audience. MHI has been participating in various 
industry consultations and investment promotion webinars, coordinated with the support 
of other entities including industry association. 
 Production Linked Incentive schemes: 
With an aim to Enhance India‟s Manufacturing Capabilities and Enhancing 
Exports – in automobile and automobile components sector, PLI Scheme for the 
automobile and automobile components sector has been notified in  September 2021.  
 
To enhance India‟s Manufacturing Capabilities and Enhancing Exports – for 
manufacture of Advance Chemistry Cell (ACC) in India, a Production -Linked Incentive 
(PLI) scheme for manufacture of Advance Chemistry Cell (ACC) in India is approve d by 
the Union Cabinet on  12th May, 2021  under Aatmanirbhar Bharat with a total outlay of 
Rs. 18,100 crores over a period of 5 years.  The Scheme has been notified on  9th June, 
2021. The PLI scheme for ACC battery envisages to incentivize large domestic and  
international players in establishing a competitive ACC battery set -up in the country. It 
represents one of the largest economic opportunities of the twenty -first century for 
several global growth sectors, such as consumer electronics, electric vehicles, and 
renewable energy. 
Regional Investment Dialogues: 
  MHI PDC has participated in multiple Regional Investment Dialogues, 
coordinated by DPIIT. These dialogues establish synergies and facilitate information 
exchange between internal stakeholders for investor promotion. 
An Empowered Group of Secretaries has been Constituted by DPIIT to provide 
support and facilitation to investors for investing in India and to boost growth in the key 
sectors of the economy. Project Development Cells (PDCs) within relevant 
Ministries/Departments of GoI have also been envisioned to ensure a faster mechanism to 
facilitate investments through integrated efforts by Central ministries and the State. In 
furtherance of above, MHI has constituted a PDC  with the  Joint Secretary (Auto)  as 
Nodal Officer with following focus areas of PDC has been mentioned:         
 

 6 
       (i) Automobile and Auto Components         
      (ii) Electric Mobility

REPORT 
 
 India‟s Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) Sector has emerged as a 
vibrant, dynamic and progressive sector of the Indian economy over the last five decades. 
MSME Sector not  only play crucial role in providing large -scale employment 
opportunities at comparatively lower capital cost than large industries but also help 
industrialization of rural and backward areas of the country, thereby, reducing regional 
imbalances, assuring more equitable distribution of national income and resources.  
MSME Sector has  strong linkages to large indu stries as ancillary units and contributes 
significantly in the inclusive industrial development of the country . MSME Sector is also 
nurturing a culture of entrepreneurship among the people of the country, especially the 
youth thereby mitigating the problem of unemployment effectively. 
 
2. MSMEs are widely spread across the country in almost all the sectors. MSMEs are 
now widening their domain across various sectors of the economy, producing diverse 
range of products and services to meet demands of domestic as well as Global markets 
and also proving to be a boon for aspiring entrepreneurs in India.  As informed by the       
M/o of MSME, the MSME Sector is providing livelihood to around 11.10 crore people of 
the country. There are a round 6.34 crore MSMEs , which contributed 27 per cent to the 
Gross Domestic Product in the year Financial Year 2020 -21.The MSME Sector has the 
huge potential to generate employment and livelihood in the rural hinterlands  of the 
country. It also has the capacity to earn foreign exchange for the exchequer through larger 
exports. 
 
3. COVID-19 pandemic had an enormous adverse impact on almost all sectors of the 
Indian economy including the MSME Sector, due to factors such as lack of funds, supply 
chain disruptions, lower productivity, non -availability of workforce etc. However, t he 
Government has adopted a multi -pronged approach covering the six pillars such as (i) 
New Enterprise Development and Employment Generation (ii) Credit Assistance and 
Capital Infusion (iii) Technological U pgradation (iv) Infrastructure & Capacity Building 
(v) Skill Development & Entrepreneurship Development T raining and (vi) Procurement 
and Marketing Support, in order to help the MSMEs to revive and regain their               
pre-pandemic growth trajectory as well as improve their economic growth. 

2 
 
Ministry of MSME  
 
4. The Ministry of MSME was formed on 9 th May, 2007 merging the erstwhile 
Ministry of Small Scale Industries and the Ministry of Agro and Rural Industries.  The 
Ministry designs policies, promotes/facilitates programmes/projects/schemes and 
monitors their implementation, with a view to assisting MSMEs and helping them to scale 
up.  
 
The major Schemes of the Ministry of MSME are mentioned as under:- 
 Prime Minister‟s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP); 
 Modified Market Development Assistance (MMDA); 
 Interest Subsidy and Eligibility Certificate (ISEC) Scheme; 
 Strengthening of Infrastructure of Existing Weak Khadi Institutions and Assistance 
for Marketing Infrastructure; 
 Credit Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE); 
 A Scheme for Promoting Innovation and Rural Entrepreneurship (ASPIRE); 
 Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI); 
 Micro and Small Enterprises–Cluster Development Programme (MSE-CDP); 
 Science & Technology (S&T); 
 Honey Mission;  
 Kumbhar Shashaktikaran Programme; 
 The National Scheduled Caste and Scheduled Tribe Hub;  
 Scheme for Promotion of MSMEs in NE Region and Sikkim; and 
 Guaranteed Emergency Credit Line (GECL).

Views/Suggestions of the Stakeholders 
 
 
16. As part of examination of the DFG (2022 -23), t he Committee had sought the 
views/suggestions of the Associations (FICCI, FISME, CII and ASSOCHAM) on the 
Government‟s target of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises contributing $2 trillion to 
the country‟s target of becoming $5 trillion economy by 2024 . The Associations apprised 
the Committee that although the Covid pandemic had adversely affected the MSME 
Sector but they are very optimistic that MSME Sector will revive quickly but it is very 
important that the blueprint laid down by the Government materializes in a time -bound 
manner. The important suggestions put forth by the Associations in this regard along with 
the recommendations of the Committee are as under:- 
 
SEPARATE POLICY FOR MEDIUM ENTERPRISES 
17. Issues of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises are different from each other and  
unified policy would not be able to treat them well as per their actual requirements.  The 
schemes need to be segregated and modified as per each of the category so that  every 
category has specific solutions. It will help enterprises to identify schemes, which are 
relevant for them. Medium sector enterprises have the potential to grow to become large 
enterprises and subsequently, these enterprises could support many other Micro & Small 
enterprises in cascading effect. If only 10% of medium enterprises could be  transformed 
into large enterprises, there would be a significant cascading effect for Micro and Small 
enterprises. Therefore, separate policy should be formulated  for Medium enterprises. At 
present, no significant scheme is  available for Medium Enterprises and given that new 

11 
 
definition is into effect, announcing special schemes for medium -sized enterprises would 
benefit numerous enterprises who have joined MSME spectre due to new definition. 
 
18. The Committee recommends that based on the divergent needs of the Medium 
Enterprises vis-à-vis Small and Micro Enterprises, it is in interest of both the 
categories to have separate and dedicated policies for better targeted development 
and growth. 
 
SETTING UP OF SME FINANCE COMPANIES 
 
19. At present, no SME Finance Companies exist in the country. Therefore, as in the 
case of infrastructure finance companies or micro-finance companies that are not engaged 
in real economic activity  but in the financing of it, SME finance  companies may  be 
established in the country. 
 
20. The Committee suggest s that SME finance companies may be established in 
the country on the lines of infrastructure finance companies or micro -finance 
companies that are not engaged in real economic activity but in financing of it. 
 
CONSULTATION WITH STAKEHOLDERS 
 
21. There is an absence of a structured need assessment  exercise before proposing and 
designing any of the major schemes. Due to weak stakeholder discussions on proposed 
schemes, the design flaws come to light too late and  also discourage potential 
implementing agencies. There is a special need for the involvement of stakeholders at the 
design stage of the  scheme to make the schemes demand driven, especially the schemes 
that are based  on SPV/consortium approach. Process of structured need assessment will 
help generate „content‟ having clarity on objectives, beneficiaries; scope and coverage of  
schemes; role and function of implementing agency. 
22. The Committee is of the view that Emphasis should be made on involvement 
of stakeholders at design stage of schemes, especially the schemes that are based on 
SPV/Consortium approach. 
GST REGIME 
 
23. The GST regime was meant to be a digitized system; however, department 
authorities still insist that separate hard copies are also provided to claim refund. This 
defeats the  purpose of digitizing process. The time involved by the MSMEs in finally 

12 
 
getting the  refund sanctioned causes a tremendous strain on the cash flows of the 
MSMEs, which in turn restricts the possibility of increasing exports. 
 
24. The Committee recommends that the GST regime should be a digitized 
system, without the requirement o f separate hard copies to be provided the 
concerned Dep artment to claim refund. This not only defeats the purpose of 
digitizing process, bu t also eases inordinate delay in getting the refund sanctioned , 
thereby resulting in tremendous strain on cash flows of the MSMEs. 
 
EMERGENCY CREDIT LINE GUARANTEE SCHEME (ECLGS) 
 
25. The Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme mandated for providing collateral 
free loans to MSMEs has been a very effective financial measure to restore their liquidity 
and financial health. The said emergency credit line has greatly helped MSMEs to restart 
operations by giving them additional working capital support. It is a welcome step of the 
Government in the Budget 2022 -23 to increase the corpus of ECLGS to Rs. 5 lakh crore 
by adding  Rs. 50 thousand crore for hospitality & related enterprises and extend the 
validity of scheme till 31st March, 2023. However, some more concerns have been raised 
by MSME, which are not able to avail the scheme. Repayment period of 3 -4 years 
including moratorium period under the scheme is very little time for MSMEs which are 
struggling to survive through second wave of Covid -19. As the cash  flow has dried, it 
would take a longer period to come back to normal liquidity and hence it is suggested that  
repayment period should be extended up to 7 – 8 years with at least 2 years of moratorium 
on principal amount. With respect to the interest, moratorium for interest from 01.03.2020 
onwards should be announced by the RBI. This accumulative interest  should be made part 
of term loan/principal amount. No interest on interest should be charged from MSMEs 
while amalgamating the interest in principal amount. 
 
26. The Committee finds that under Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme, 
repayment period of 3 -4 years including moratorium period is a very short period 
for MSMEs, which are struggling to survive from the second wave of Covid -19. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the repayment period should be extended 
upto 7 -8 years with at least 2 years of moratorium on principal amount. With 

13 
 
respect to the interest, moratorium for interest from 01.03.2020 onwards should be 
announced by RBI. 
 
 
 
CREDIT GUARANTEE FUND TRUST FOR MICRO AND SMALL 
ENTERPRISES (CGTMSE) 
 
27. During the budget 2022-23, it was announced by the Hon‟ble Finance Minister that 
the CGTMSE Scheme shall be revamped and Rs. 2 lakh crore will also be infused in the  
scheme. It is indeed a welcome step in the direction to make this scheme more viable  and 
convenient for its stakeholders including MSEs. As the scheme is to be revamped,  it has 
been requested that the limit of collateral free loans under this scheme, either term loan or 
working capital loan, should be increased from existing Rs. 2 crore to upto Rs. 5 crores, 
irrespective of the constitution (Private Ltd ., LLP, Partnership and/or proprietorship) of 
applicant MSEs provided all other criteria are fulfilled. 
 
28. The Committee is in consonance with the suggestion of Associations and 
recommends that while revamping the CGTMSE scheme, the limit of collateral free 
loans under this scheme, either term loan or working capital loan should be 
increased from the existing R s. 2 crore upto Rs. 5 crores, irrespective of the 
Constitution (Private Ltd., LLP, Partnership and/or Proprietorship) of applicant 
MSE’s provided all other criteria are fulfilled. 
 
AATMANIRBHAR BHARAT 
 
29. Government is focusing upon Make in India, which is entirely appreciable effort as 
it helps MSMEs to grow. It is a fact that India is importing MSME oriented products in  
huge quantity, which can be manufactured in India. One of the reasons behind this  could 
be explained as lack of awareness amongs t MSMEs about the products that are  being 
imported in the country. Feedback has been received from the industry that  Government 
should put out a list of such products along with their production  specifications so that 
enterprises become excited about getting into the production of such products. Such 
imported products should also carry the information about their  market potential in the 
country. This would be beneficial for a large number of potential entrepreneurs who wish 
to set up new manufacturing enterprises. A Central Market  Intelligence Center for import 

14 
 
related products and components would be of great  help to MSMEs to achieve the goal of 
Aatmanirbhar Bharat. Soft loans at minimal  interest rate of 3 -4% with a minimum tenure 
of 9-10 years for repayment period, Easy land acquisition, less compliances could be key 
factors in developing domestic manufacturing with MSMEs. Till the domestic 
manufacturing is strengthened, high  import restrictions should be avoided and only, if 
necessary, it should be applied in phased manner. 
 
30. The Committee understands that a number of MSME oriented products are 
presently being imported , which can be manufactured in India. The Committee , 
therefore, recommends that a Central Market Intelligence Centre for import related 
products and components be set up in the country. The said Centre may be 
entrusted with the task of putting out a list of products , which are being imported 
alongwith their specificat ions and spreading awareness of the same through 
electronic, print and social media to attract interested entrepreneurs to set up new 
manufacturing enterprises in MSME Sector, thereby fulfilling the Government ’s 
vision of Aatmanirbhar Bharat. 
 
TESTING AND CERTIFICATION FACILITIES IN TECHNOLOGY CENTRES  
31. For any business to flourish, it is important that products are of certain standards 
and excel in quality. For exports, MSMEs need to meet a certain required international or  
regional specific standard for which adequate facilities are not available in the country. 
Besides, available testing facilities are costly , which MSMEs cannot afford. Testing &  
Certifications should be made convenient and cheaper for MSMEs. The country has 
arobust infrastructure of  technology centers that are supporting MSMEs in many ways.  
The Associations have received very positive feedback about these technology centers 
and Ministry of MSME must be congratulated for running this facility across the country. 
Keeping this network i n view, suggestion s have also been received that Technology 
Centers could also be utilised to facilitate subsidised testing for regional  MSMEs. A 
mechanism/tie-up should be developed that testing can be done in India at these 
technology Centers whereas cer tificates for the same test could be issued from  various 
global testing centers , which are acceptable in respective countries/regions.  Ministry of 
MSME could do tie-ups with various global agencies through its technology centers.  
 
32. The Committee recommends that the existing Technology Centres should also 
be used to facilitate subsidi sed testing and certification of regional MSMEs. Further 

15 
 
a mechanism should be devised by the Ministry to tie up with global Testing Centres 
whose certificates are acceptable in respective countries/regions. The Committee 
hopes that this new arrangement will not only ease the testing process and reduce 
the cost, but also encourage new entrepreneurs to come up with more innovations.

introduced to mobilize the funds from banking institutions in order to cater to the 
additional fund requirement of Khadi and Village Industries Institutions. For this, an

is assessing the recycling of working capital (working cycle) @ 16 months but on the 
other hand the banks are calculating it at 4 months and this is the bone of contention 
between KVIC and banks and this situation is affecting the ISEC Scheme adversely. The

banks for bringing uniformity between the methodology used by KVIC to issue ISEC 
certificate and the working capital calculation methodology adopted by banks for bridging 
the gaps between ISEC being certified by KVIC and working capital amount sanctioned 
by banks, as the issue is a long standing one.   The Ministry informed the Committee that 
the Chief Advisor (Cost), Ministry of Finance, Gov ernment of India conducted a study to 
ascertain an appropriate Working Capital Formula for ISEC Scheme. The study report has 
been placed in a consultation meeting conducted with representatives of major  Khadi 
Institutions/federations and other stakeholders of Khadi  programme. The representatives 
of Khadi institutions/Federations present in the meeting unanimously opposed the 
shortening of the operating cycle for working capital for the Khadi  programme and for 
retaining the existing Working Capital Formula and further suggested for the conduct of a

study considering the peculiarity of working conditions/decentralized nature of activities 
of Khadi sector. Subsequently, the matter was also discussed with the Bankers who were 
of the view that the KVIC‟s ISEC working capital formula should be modified/brought 
down for acceptance of banking norms.  Further, a committee has been constituted to 
study the existing working capital formula. 
 
58. The Committee observes that the actual Interest Subsidy Eligibility 
Certificates issued and funds released by Banks are not very encouraging and 
creates gap in working capital requirement and actual fund availability as a result of 
which the Khadi Institutions fail to achieve the desired level of performance.  It has 
been brought to the notice of the Committee time and again that KVIC and banks 
are adopting a different working capital formula.  KVIC is assessing the recycling of 
working capital (working cycle) @ 16 months but on the other hand the banks are 
calculating it at 4 months and this is the bone of contention between KVIC and 
banks, which appears to be one of the lacuna e for the gap existing between ISEC 
issued and Bank finance .  T he Committee observes that this issue needs to be 
addressed at the appropriate level.  The Committee strongly recommends that a n 
amicable formula may be devised by KVIC and banks, which is acceptable to both 
in order to increase the efficiency and efficacy of the ISEC scheme.

Credit Crunch in MSME Sector 
 
90. During the examination of Demands for Grants (2022 -23), the Committee sought a 
response from the Ministry whether the Ministry had carried out any study to assess the 
formal credit availed by MSME Sector and whether there has been a gap between credit 
actually disbursed vis-a-vis the total demand and the steps t aken by the Ministry to bridge 
the gap between the disbursement and credit demand. In response, the Ministry informed 
the Committee that according to the International Finance Corporation (IFC) Report, 
"Financing India‟s MSMEs", November 2018, the addressa ble credit gap for the MSME 
Sector stood at Rs. 25,80,000  crores. Further, based on the said IFC Report, the Expert 
Committee on Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, constituted by the Reserve Bank of 
India in December, 2018, under the chairmanship of Shri  U.K. Sinha also estimated the 

33 
 
overall credit gap in the MSME sector to be in the range of Rs. 20 lakh crore to Rs. 25 
lakh crore. 
 
91. The Ministry further apprised the Committee that various initiatives had been 
undertaken by RBI to increase the credit f low to the Sector, the details of which are as 
follows:- 
 A target of 7.5 percent of Adjusted Net Banking Credit (ANBC) or Credit 
Equivalent Amount of Off Balance Sheet Exposure, whichever is higher, has been 
prescribed for Scheduled Commercial Banks (SCBs)  for lending to Micro 
Enterprises.  
 SCBs have been mandated not to accept collateral security in the case of loans up to 
Rs. 10 lakh extended to units in the MSE sector. 
 To solve the problem of delayed payment to MSMEs, RBI has come out with the 
guidelines for setting up and operating the Trade Receivables Discounting System 
(TReDS). The scheme is for setting up and operating the institutional mechanism to 
facilitate the financing of trade receivables of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises 
(MSMEs) from corporate and other buyers, including Government departments and 
Public Sector Undertakings (PSUs) through multiple financiers. 
 
 
92.   The Committee was apprised that with a  view to reaching out to MSE entrepreneurs, 
Regional Offices of RBI had been advised to organize two/three Town hall meetings in a 
year in MSME clusters, preferably unbanked/underbanked clusters. The objective of the 
Town hall meetings is to create awarene ss of banking facilities among MSEs and linking 
them to the formal banking system. 
 
93. The Committee noticed that overall credit gap in the MSME Sector is in the 
range of Rs. 20 lakh crore to Rs. 25 lakh crore.  The Committee observes that 
MSME Sector hol ds the key to make the Nation an economic superpower and 
MSMEs are critical to unlocking the potential of India envisioned under the 
'Aatmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan' campaign and in an endeavour to make India        
$5 trillion economy by 2024 .  The Committee  recommends that remedial steps 
should be taken by the Government to bridge the credit gap of the MSME sector , 
which may prove to be very beneficial for the overall strengthening of MSME Sector 
and also address the problem of credit crunch of MSME Sector. 
 
 

34 
 
94. The Committee observes that a large chunk of Micro enterprises are 
operating in an informal sector and therefore they are not eligible for formal credit 
offered by financial institutions and these Micro enterprises are often deprived of 
benefits announced by the Government under various schemes meant for MSMEs. 
Another reason is lack of awareness among the Micro entrepreneurs because most of 
the times the intended beneficiaries either know very little about the various schemes 
or know nothing to take advantage of it. The Committee recommends that adequate 
remedial steps should be taken by the Government to bring these informal Micro 
enterprises in the formal sector by offering various incentives for t hem and by 
creating adequate awareness among them about various schemes offered by 
Government for their welfare.   
 
 
95. The Committee observes that there is no updated data about MSMEs in the 
country.  Further, t here is lack of  data about manufacturing activities in th e 
country.  In the absence of adequate and granular data, the policies and guidelines 
that the Government frames often misfire.  The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that data should be collected about the MSMEs in  the country and thereafter 
policies and guidelines should be designed for the benefit of MSMEs accordingly. 
 
96. The MSME Sector of India is considered as growth engine of the nation. The 
Committee feels that if nurtured properly, the MSME sector has the potential to 
make India an economic superpower.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that 
proper attention must be paid for the all -round development of MSME Sector and 
Government may try to increase the contribution of MSME s in the National 
economy.

 Enhancing guarantee products towards increased greening and gender participation ;

counterpart funding by the Government of India through Budgetary support. 
 
Design of the programme:   
 
 
100. The programme has identified two results areas viz:-  
 
(i) Strengthening Institutions and Governance of the MSME Programme. 
(ii) Support to Market Access, Firm Capabilities and Access to Finance.

building platforms for the provision of critical services to MSMEs and enhancing 
outcomes from competitiveness related schemes. RAMP is designed to support 
selected ongoing M /o MSME support programmes, particularly focusing on the 
competitiveness aspects.

capacities of MSMEs with administrative, financial, infrastructural and           
techno-managerial support , which is y et to be launched on the ground. T he 

36 
 
programme is expected to develop and upscale MSMEs at least in the focal States

perusal as and when these are available.

facilitate expansion and growth of MSME enterprises , increasing the investment 
limit under the new definition allows MSMEs to invest in plant an d machinery for 
growth without the fear of losing the status.  Further, the increased limit also enables 
MSMEs to invest in new technologies to enhance their producti vity.  It also removes 
the distinction between MSMEs in the manufacturing as well as services sector and 
increases the country’s exports through MSMEs. The Committee appreciates the 
Government’s decision to modify the definition of M icro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises as detailed above at para no.  5, as per the long -standing demand of 
Industry Associations.  The Committee also welcomes the decision to include retail 
and wholesale trade under the purview of MSME, thereby enabling them to get 
priority sector lending.

that allocation to both DC -MSME and ARI Division of the Mi nistry has been

(Para 47) 
 
19. PMEGP is one of the flagship Schemes of the Ministry of MSME , which is 
capable of generating large -scale employment for youth of the country, especially at 
this time of scarcity of employment in the country as a consequence of the Pandemic. 
The Committee , therefore, recommends that Ministry should ask for more 
allocations at the RE stage for effective implementation of the Scheme  in order to 
create large-scale employment for the workforce of the country. 
 
(Para 49) 

42 
 
 
20. The Committee is concerned to note that out of the total number of 
applications received under the Scheme, around 36% of the total applications were 
rejected by the banks, only 25% of the applications got sanctioned by the banks and 
a meager 1 8% of applications got disbursements by the banks. Since PMEGP 
Scheme is one of the flagship Schemes of the Ministry, the Committee recommends 
that the Ministry should look into the matter and take ste ps for removing the 
hindrances and simplify  the procedures with minimal formalities and technicalities 
so as to ensure that off take of loan under the scheme is improved. 
 
(Para 50) 
 
21. During the course of Committee meetings, Members had raised the issue  of 
banks’ lukewarm and unfriendly response towards borrowers, which often deter 
them to approach the banks for loans.  The Committee recommends that banks 
should adopt a friendly and favourable approach towards borrowers and make 
them aware about various schemes available for availing loans.  Separate windows 
for facilitating MSMEs may also be introduced in the banks for facilitating 
entrepreneurs. 
 
(Para 51) 
 
22. The Committee observes that the actual Interest Subsidy Eligibility 
Certificates issued and funds released by Banks are not very encouraging and 
creates gap in working capital requirement and actual fund availability as a result of 
which the Khadi Institutions fail to achieve the desired level of performance.  It has 
been brought to t he notice of the Committee time and again that KVIC and banks 
are adopting a different working capital formula.  KVIC is assessing the recycling of 
working capital (working cycle) @ 16 months but on the other hand the banks are 
calculating it at 4 months a nd this is the bone of contention between KVIC and 
banks, which appears to be one of the lacuna e for the gap existing between ISEC 
issued and Bank finance .  The Committee observes that this issue needs to be 
addressed at the appropriate level.  The Committee strongly recommends that a n 
amicable formula may be devised by KVIC and banks, which is acceptable to both 
in order to increase the efficiency and efficacy of the ISEC scheme. 
 
(Para 58) 
 
23. The Committee observes that the ISEC issued and bank finance provided to 
the Institutions is yet to reach its full potential . The Committee , therefore, 
recommends that remedial measures should be taken by the Ministry to address the 
issues and create awareness drive through various available modes to popularize the 
Scheme to increase the off take .  The procedures may be simplified, formalities may 
be kept at minimum, and banks may be educated about the Scheme and advised to 

43 
 
adopt friendly and favourable app roach while considering the applications and 
claims. 
 
(Para 59) 
 
24. The Committee notes that the BE for SFURTI Scheme for FY 2022 -23is Rs. 
334crore but the Actual Expenditure as on 31.02.2022 is Rs. 200.20 crore as against 
RE of Rs. 406.02 crore for FY 2021-22, which means Ministry have spent 49 per cent 
amount only. The Committee expresses its concern over the underutilization of 
funds by the Minist ry for such an important scheme, which is capable of generating 
employment in a large scale in the rural areas for the artisans, particularly during 
the Pandemic  period. The Committee recommends that Ministry must ensure that 
budget earmarked for SFURTI sc heme are utilized quarterly and planned manner 
and exhausted fully for effective implementation of the scheme in rural areas for 
benefit of the traditional artisans. 
 
(Para 63) 
 
25. The Committee also expresses concern that during the second and the third 
waves of Covid -19 Pandemic MSME sector was once again badly hit resulting in 
number of people losing their livelihood.  The Committee is of the view that SFURTI 
has potential to generate large -scale employment in the rural areas of the country 
with less in vestment.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Ministry 
should set up more SFURTI clusters throughout the country to promote 
employment generation thereby mitigating the hardships caused due to Covid -19 
Pandemic. 
 
(Para 64) 
 
26. The Committee notes that the BE, RE & AE for Coir Vikas Yojana for 
Financial Years 2018-19, 2019-20,2020-21 and 2021-22 had been static (except in BE 
2020-21) and no significant enhancement in the outlays is taking place. The 
Committee observes that Coir V ikas Yojana is one such scheme of the Ministry, 
which is capable of nurturing an entrepreneurship culture among the aspiring 
entrepreneurs thereby generate employment of the youth. The Committee 
recommends that more budgetary outlays may be earmarked for s uch a good 
scheme implemented by the Ministry and in the current FY, an enhanced budget 
may be demanded by the Ministry at RE stage for making it a meaningful and 
fruitful scheme, keeping in view the fact that the amount allocated at RE stage has 
been more or less actually been spent.   
 
(Para 69) 
 

44 
 
27. The Committee observes that one of the most important objectives of the 
implementation of various Schemes under Coir Board is the creation of employment, 
especially in rural areas of the country.  For this purpose, Coir Board is providing 
training on various aspects of production and development of new/innovative 
products. The Committee recommends that Ministry should make these training 
courses popular th rough various social publicity media  available so that large 
number of people , especially from younger generation may get attracted to such 
training courses , which will culminate in fruitful employment  to the unemployed 
youth of the country. 
 
(Para 70) 
 
28. The Committee notes that export performance of coir and coir products 
during 2019-20 was not encouraging  due to Covid Pandemic and consequent 
lockdowns but thereafter in 2020 -21, the targets were achieved by Coir Board. The 
Committee appreciates the efforts made by Coir Board in restoring the performance 
and display of resilience.  The Committee recommends th at a contingency plan and 
strategy should be devised by Coir Board in order to tackle such unforeseen 
situations like Covid pandemic in order to shield the Coir Sector from disaster as 
witnessed during 2019-20. Further, the Committee recommends that high t argets for 
exports should be set and endeavour should be made to achieve those targets by 
effective planning and execution. Latest technology and techniques should be 
adopted for making coir products more competitive to meet the international 
standards. 
 
(Para 71) 
 
29. The Committee notes that during the Covid-induced lockdowns, MSMEs were 
adversely affected due to the shortage of raw material and their businesses incurred 
losses. The Committee, therefore, recommends that a robust procurement system 
should be evolved , which could ensure unhindered and timely supply of raw 
materials to MSMEs at reasonable prices so that there is no scarcity of raw material 
supply to MSMEs. The Committee is also of the view that the Ministry should also 
explore other available options fo r raw material supply to MSMEs instead of 
becoming solely dependent on NSIC in coordination with other concerned 
Ministries/Departments to meet the requirement of MSMEs. 
 
(Para 73) 
 
30. The Livelihood Business Incubators (LBI), Technology Business Incubato rs 
(TBI) and Technology Centers  under NSIC have been a source of employment for 
youth of the country. Further, NSIC through its Incubation Centres provides 
training to the prospective entrepreneurs in the manufacturing as well as service 
sector for skill development and employment purposes. The Committee recommends 

45 
 
that more LBIs/TBIs/Incubation Centres should be established in cooperation with 
State Governments so that training on conventional as well as hi -tech trades are 
imparted to entrepreneurs for the ir skill development in areas of business operation 
for their gainful employment. 
 
(Para 74) 
 
31. The Committee observes that under National SC/ST Hub, the Actual 
Expenditure often has been less than the BE  & RE. The Committee is concerned 
about the under -utilization of allocated funds meant for the marginalized 
communities of the society. The Committee recommends that Ministry should 
endeavor to improve the situation by ensuring that the budget earmarked for SC/ST  
Hub Scheme is utilized fully for the intended beneficiaries. Lack of awareness 
among the SC/ST entrepreneurs may be one of the main reasons for lower availment 
of various benefits offered under the scheme , hence efforts may be made to create 
awareness among SC/ST entrepreneurs through various available modes like print 
or social media etc. Handholding of SC/ST entrepreneurs may work well in 
improving the performance of this scheme. U nderutilization of funds  is a serious 
cause of concern for the Committee; therefore, Ministry is advised to ensure full 
utilization of funds. 
 
(Para 79) 
 
32. The Committee hopes that the Champions Scheme achieves its targeted 
purpose for which it has been introduced and performs well and proves to be 
beneficial for the MSME Sector.  The Committee desires that Committee may be 
apprised of the guidelines and all the important details of the Champions Schemes 
after the approval is accorded for the same. 
 
(Para 84) 
 
33. The Committee appreciates the introduction of GECL Scheme, which aims to 
meet the liquidity demand of the MSMEs in this critical time of pandemic and it 
hopes that the GECL Scheme proves successful and beneficial for the intended 
beneficiaries for the over all strengthening of MSMEs.  The Committee recommends 
that all the formalities and procedures of the scheme may be kept simple and 
convenient for the MSMEs for increasing off take and provide full advantage of the 
scheme to them.  The Committee desires tha t the details of all the modalities, 
progress made and utilization of funds allocated under GECL Scheme should be 
furnished to the Committee for its perusal. 
 
(Para 89) 
 

46 
 
34. The Committee noticed that overall credit gap in the MSME Sector is in the 
range of Rs. 20 lakh crore to Rs. 25 lakh crore.  The Committee observes that 
MSME Sector holds the key to make the Nation an economic superpower and 
MSMEs are critical to unlocking the potential of India env isioned under the 
'Aatmanirbhar Bharat Abhiyan' campaign and in an endeavour to make India        
$5 trillion economy by 2024 .  The Committee recommends that remedial steps 
should be taken by the Government to bridge the credit gap of the MSME sector, 
which may prove to be very beneficial for the overall strengthening of MSME Sector 
and also address the problem of credit crunch of MSME Sector. 
 
(Para 93) 
 
35. The Committee observes that a large chunk of Micro enterprises are 
operating in an informal sector and therefore they are not eligible for formal credit 
offered by financial institutions and these Micro enterprises are often deprived of 
benefits announced by the Government under various schemes meant for MS MEs. 
Another reason is lack of awareness among the Micro entrepreneurs because most of 
the times the intended beneficiaries either know very little about the various schemes 
or know nothing to take advantage of it. The Committee recommends that adequate 
remedial steps should be taken by the Government to bring these informal Micro 
enterprises in the formal sector by offering various incentives for them and by 
creating adequate awareness among them about various schemes offered by 
Government for their welfare.   
 
(Para 94) 
 
36. The Committee observes that there is no updated data about MSMEs in the 
country.  Further, t here is lack of  data about manufacturing activities in th e 
country.  In the absence of adequate and granular data, the policies and guidelines 
that the Government frames often misfire.  The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that data should be collected about the MSMEs in the country and thereafter 
policies and guidelines should be designed for the benefit of MSMEs accordingly. 
 
(Para 95) 
 
37. The MSME Sector of India is considered as growth engine of the nation. The 
Committee feels that if nurtured properly, the MSME sector has the potential to 
make India an economic superpower.  Therefore, the Committee recommends that 
proper attention must be paid for the all -round development of MSME Sector and 
Government may try to increase the contribution of MSME s in the National 
economy. 
 
(Para 96) 
 

47 
 
38. The Committee recommends that a countrywide comprehensive study needs 
to be conducted on the adverse impact of Covid pandemic on MSME Sector in order 
to devise action plan and strategy to shield and strengthen the MSME Sector. The 
findings of the report may also be shared with the Committee for perusal. 
 
(Para 97) 
 
39. The Committee observes that as per the information available, RAMP is a 
multi-faceted initiative of the Government assisted by the World Bank to develop 
capacities of MSMEs with administrative, financial, infrastructural and           
techno-managerial support , which is y et to be launched on the ground. T he 
programme is expected to develop and upscale MS MEs at least in the focal States 
and MSME Associations are eagerly wait ing for launching of the programme and 
capture the pay -offs. The Committee notes that a weakness of the programme  may 
prove to be reliance on Government machinery and agencies for imple mentation of 
planned interventions. These agencies and offices are already implementing the 
respective schemes and notwithstanding the handholding and capacity building by 
global experts, under the aegis of World Bank, scope for improvements may be 
limited. The Committee recommends that following global practices , MSME 
federations and stakeholders may also be involved in implementation of the 
programme components under guidance and supervision of the Government. Th e 
Committee further recommends that the inf ormation about the progress made and 
the modalities of the RAMP Scheme may also be furnished to the Committee for its 
perusal as and when these are available. 
 
(Para 102)

REPORT 
The Heavy Industries in India is mainly dominated by Heavy Engineering, Machine 
Tools, Heavy Electrical and Automotive Industries. The Automotive Industry which 
contributes 6.4 % to India’s GDP is one of the key drivers of the Indian economy. Further, 
12% of the total manufacturing activities in India is contributed by the Capital Goods Sector 
comprising Heavy Engineering and Machine Tools Industry, which translates to 1.5% of 
GDP. These Sectors are therefore crucial for development of India’s economy. However, the 
COVID-19 pandemic had a huge adverse impact on all sectors of the economy. The onset of 
the second wave of the pandemic and the continuing threat of Omicron has affected the 
already struggling India’s journey to prosperity. The Union Budget 2022 -23 is the second 
Budget amidst the challenges of the new variants of Covid -19, changing geo -political 
relations and the uncertainties in the global economy. Budget 2022 is hailed as a growth -
oriented Budget focused on building long term strengt h using investment as the growth lever 
while maintaining policy stability and inclusivity.   A host of measures have been announced 
in the Budget for  various Sectors which aims at boosting growth amidst high and rising 
inflation and continuing Covid. The m ain focus of the Budget this year are PM Gati Shakti, 
Inclusive Development, Productivity Enhancement, Energy Transition, Climate Action, 
Financing of Investment s etc.  PM Gati Shakti project aims to take  India’s logistics, 
infrastructure, sustainability a nd green mobility initiatives forward.  The decision to expand 
Capex target by 35.4% from Rs. 5.54 lakh crore to Rs. 7.50 lakh crore is expected to propel 
the economic growth of the country.  
2. The Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on In dustry considered 
and examined the Demands for Grants (2022 -23) of the Ministry of Heavy Industries in its 
meeting held on 18th February, 2022. 
Ministry of Heavy Industry (MHI) 
3. The Ministry of Heavy Industries promotes the d evelopment and growth of three 
Sectors i.e. Capital Goods (Heavy Engineering Equipment and Machine Tools Industry) , 
Automobile and Heavy Electrical Equipment  Sectors in the country and  administers 24 
Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) and  4 Autonomous Organizations. The CP SEs 
under the Ministry  are engaged in manufacturing, consultancy and contracting services.  
These CPSEs manufacture a wide range of products viz. Boilers, Gas/Steam/Hydro Turbines, 
Industrial Machinery, Turbo Generators and Consumer Products such as Tea and  Salt. The 
Ministry also  supports the development of a range of Intermediate Engineering Industry such 
as Castings, Forgings, Diesel Engines, Industrial Gears and Gear-Boxes. 

2 
 
4. The Ministry maintains a constant dialogue with various Industry Associations  in the 
Capital Goods, Automobile and Heavy Electrical Equipment Sector and encourages 
initiatives for the growth of industry in these areas. The Ministry also assists the industries in 
achieving their growth plans through policy support, and other interve ntions such as 
advocating rationalization of tariff, promoting technological collaboration, research & 
development activities etc. 
 
Vision and Mission of MHI 
5. According to the Annual Report 2021 -22 of the Ministry of Heavy Industries, the 
following is their Vision & Mission: 
Vision 
"To have globally competitive, green & technology -driven heavy industry 
manufacturing sector, including automotive and capital good sectors, which propels 
growth and job creation" 
Mission 
"To facilitate Auto, Heavy Electrical  & Capital Goods Sectors to be globally 
competitive, growth oriented and profitable and to provide all necessary support to 
CPSEs to improve their overall performance".

Overview of the Automotive Industry  
12. The automobile industry is one of the key drivers of the Indian economy. There is a 
presence of almost every global auto manufacturer in the country. India is  the largest 
manufacturer of 2W, 3W and 4th largest manufacturers of passenger cars in the world. Indian 
Tractor Industry is the largest in the world (excluding sub 20 HP belt driven tractors used in 
China), accounting for one third of the global productio n. Indian Tractors were exported to 
US and other countries like Malaysia, Turkey, etc.  The industry produced about 22 million 
vehicles including Passenger Vehicles, Commercial Vehicles, Three Wheelers, Two 
Wheelers and Quadricycles in financial year 2020-21 and about 16 million vehicles have 
been produced during the April 2021 to December 2021. 
13. The Indian auto component industry, with a well evolved manufacturing ecosystem, 
produces a wide variety of products including engine parts, drive transmis sion and steering 
parts, body and chassis, suspension and braking parts, equipment and electrical parts, besides 
others to service the dynamic automobile industry . As informed by the MHI during the 
examination of Demands for Grants 2022 -23, the auto compon ent industry provides di rect 
employment to  85 lakh people and indirect employment to 2.9 crore people.   Further, the 
automotive  industry  contributes 6.4%  to India’s GDP and 35%  to  manufacturing GDP.

for all cars in India.  The Committee has been informed by the Automobile Associations  
that: 
 With the recently implemented advanced crash norms, India is at par with Europe in 
terms of regulations for vehicle safety. This is despite the per capita income in India 
being 20 times lower than that in Europe.  
 Nowhere in the world are 6 air bags mandatory.  

14 
 
 There is no reliable official data in India to determine the benefits of 6 airbags. 
However, there are sufficient global studies which suggest that air bags can be 
counterproductive, more fatal, can lead to more injuries if seat belts are not worn. And

specially on the rear seats is negligible.

support the ongoing  programmes of the Government, focusing on competitive aspect of 
MSMEs.

1. The Committee further notes that the Ministry has been able to utilize  99.62 
percentage of the reduced revised allocation of Rs. 900 crore for the financial year 2020-
21.  As regards  the present financial year 2021 -22, MHI could utilize Rs. 952.66 crore

the Ministry of Heavy Industries which oversees important CPSEs, Heavy Electrical 
Equipments and Auto Sector etc. should ensure that the entire RE is fully utilized in the 
remaining period of the financial year and should  henceforth rationalize the 
expenditure spreading all through the year to avoid uneven spending.
