Recommendation/Observation 
29. The Committee is deeply concerned to note that the MHI has been 
allocated a meagr e amount of Rs 200.25 crore for Development of Capital 
Goods Sector, one of the important sectors,  against the projection of 498.75 
crore, which is less than 50% of the actual amount demanded by the 
Ministry. The Committee is of the view that the Capital Goods sector is of 
the strategic and economic importance due to its capability to boost growth 
in the manufacturing sector and the overall economy and emphasis should 
be laid on building a globally competitive, self -reliant and sustainable 
Capital Goods Sector. The Committee therefore feels that  there is an urgent 
need for creating an ecosystem for export promotion, investment, 
technology, automation and driving new sustainable solutions which is 
crucial for accelerating India’s growth trajectory and harne ssing the full 
potential. The Committee strongly believes that Capital Goods industry is 
one of the key pillars of the Production -Linked Incentives (PLIs) to boost 
manufacturing sector growth by leveraging the emerging opportunities and 
further boosting gr owth in the Indian economy. Since the BE 2022 -23 
allocations are less than even half of the projected amount of Rs. 498.75 
crore for the Development Capital Goods Sector,  the Committee is of the 
view that to cater to the needs of the entire Capital Goods industry across 
the country, the BE allocation of Rs 200.25 crore would not be adequate. 
The Committee, therefore, recommends that MHI should address the issue of 
huge curtailment of funds for Development of Capital Goods Sector and  
seek enhanced allocati on at RE stage  so as to promote the growth and 
development of the Capital  Goods  Sector.

REPORT 
 
 The Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) sector has emerged as a highly 
vibrant and dynamic sector of the Indian economy over the last five decades. It contributes 
significantly in the economic and social development of the country by fostering 
entrepreneurship and generating large employment opportunities at comparatively lower 
capital cost, next only to agriculture. The MSMEs are complementary to large industries a s 
ancillary units and  this sector contributes significantly in the inclusive industrial 
development of the country.  The MSMEs are widening their domain across sectors of the 
economy, producing diverse range of products and services to meet demands of domes tic as 
well as global markets. As informed by the Ministry of MSME, the MSME sector has 
contributed 27 per cent to GDP in the FY2020-21, 36 per cent to Manufacturing Output in 
the FY2020-21, second largest employer after agriculture with 6.34 crore MSMEs providing 
employment to 11.10 crore persons and contributed 45 per cent to Export in the FY2021-22. 
  
2. The MSMEs have been contributing significantly to  the expansion of entrepreneurial 
endeavors through business innovations. The MSMEs in India are also playing a crucial role 
by providing large employment opportunities at comparatively lower capital cost than large 
industries as well as through industrialization of rural & backward  areas, inter alia, reducing 
regional imbalances, assuring more equitable d istribution of  national income and  wealth. 
Besides, the Ministry is working towards an agenda of inclusive development, and has taken 
various initiatives and measures to ensure that demographically as well as geographically 
weaker sections are benefitted for their overall development. 
  
Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises 
 
3. The Ministry of Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises (MSME) envisions a 
progressive MSME sector by promoting growth and development of the Sector, including 
Khadi, Village and  Coir Industries, in cooperation with concerned Ministries/Departments, 
State Governments and other Stakeholders, through providing support to existing 
enterprises, adopting cutting edge technologies and encouraging creation of new 
enterprises. A number of statutory and non-statutory bodies work under the aegis of the 
Ministry of MSME. These include the Khadi and Village Industries Commission (KVIC) 
and the Coir Board besides National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC), National 
Institute for  Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (NIMSME) and Mahatma Gandhi 
Institute for Rural Industrialisation (MGIRI).   
 
  

2  
4. The Ministry of MSME runs various schemes aimed at financial assistance, 
technology assistance and upgradation, infrastructure development, skill development and 
training, enhancing competitiveness and market assistance of MSMEs. The major schemes 
of the Ministry of MSME are as under: 
 
(i) Prime Minister‟s Employment Generation Programme (PMEGP) 
(ii) Credit Guarantee Trust Fund For Micro and Small Enterprises(CGTMSE) - 
 Provision of Collateral Free Credit for MSMEs 
(iii) A Scheme for Promotion of Innovation, Rural Industries & Entrepreneurship 
 (ASPIRE) 
(iv) Entrepreneurship and Skill Development Programme (ESDP) 
(v) Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional Industries (SFURTI) 
(vi) Micro and Small Enterprises-Cluster Development Programme (MSE-CDP) 
(vii) Scheme for providing financial assistance to Khadi institutions under MPDA 
(viii) MSME Champions Scheme (erstwhile CLCS-TUS) 
(ix) Raising and Accelerating MSME Performance (RAMP) Scheme 
 
New Definition of MSME 
 
5. In accordance with the provision of Micro, Small & Medium Enterprises 
Development (MSMED) Act, 2006, the Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises (MSME) are 
classified as below: 
(i) a micro enterprise, where the investment in plan t and machinery or equipment 
does  not exceed one crore rupees and turnover does not exceed five crore 
rupees; 
(ii) a small enterprise, where the investment in plant and machinery or equipment 
does  not exceed ten crore rupees and turnover does not exceed fifty crore 
rupees; and 
(iii) a medium enterprise, where the investment in plant and machinery or 
equipment  does not exceed fifty crore rupees and turnover does not exceed 
two hundred and fifty  crore rupees. 
 
6. The new classification has come into effect from 1st July, 2020. The earlier criteria 
of classification of MSMEs under MSMED Act, 2006 were based on investment in plant 
and machinery/equipment. It was different for manufacturing and service units. It was also  
very low in terms of financial limits. Since then , the economy has undergone significant  
changes. A revision in MSME criteria of classification was announced under Atma Nirbhar  
Bharat package on 13th May, 2020. This has been done in order to be realistic with time 

3  
and to establish an objective system of classification and to provide ease of doing business. 
The turnover with respect to exports will not be counted in the limits of turnover for any 
category of MSME units which will offer major relief to the exporters. 
 
7. The primary responsibility of promotion and development of MSMEs is of the State 
Governments. However, the Government of India, supplements efforts of the State 
Governments through various initiatives. The role of the Ministry of MSME and its 
organisations is to assist the States in their efforts to encourage entrepreneurship, 
employment and livelihood opportunities and enhance the competitiveness of MSMEs in  
the changed economic scenario. 
 
8. The Committee is of the view that the new classification of MSMEs would bring 
about positive changes in the MSME Sector including many benefits that will aid 
MSMEs to grow in size  by attracting investments and would generate more 
employment opportunities. In this regard, in the deposition by the Secretary, Ministry 
of MSME on 20.02.2023 before the Committee, it emerged that although the change in 
definition of MSMEs is for their benefit, however,  a study is required for sector-wise 
segregation of  the MSM Es. The Committee  recommends that the Minist ry should 
carry out a study for sector -wise segregation of  the MSMEs in order to ensure 
targeted distribution of budgetary allocation s which w ould facilitate development, 
expansion and growth of the MSME sector.  
 
Dream of Five Trillion Dollar Economy and the MSME Sector 
 
9.      To achieve the set target of becoming the $5 trillion economy by 2024, t he 
Government is implementing various schemes, programmes and initiatives for the 
promotion, development and enhancing the competiveness of MSME sector in the country. 
A number of recent initiatives have been taken to strengthen, support, finance , revive and 
reconstruct MSMEs such as:  
(i) Rs. 5 lakh crore Emergency Credit Line Guarantee Scheme (ECLGS), for 
businesses, including MSMEs was announced as a part of Atma Nirbhar Bharat 
Package with initial guarantee coverage of Rs. 3 lakh crore on 13.05.2020 with 
validity of scheme up to 30.11.2020. Subsequently, this was extended with 
infusion of Rs. 1.5 lakh crore on 29.09.2021 with validity of scheme up to 
31.03.2022 and with infusion of Rs. 50,000 crore on 01.02.2022 with validity of 
scheme up to 31.03.2023.  
(ii) Rs. 50,000 crore equity infusion through Self Reliant India (SRI) Fund. This 
scheme has a provision of Rs.10,000 crore from Government of India and Rs. 

4  
40,000 cro re leverage through Private Equity/Venture Capital funds. This 
initiative is aimed at providing growth capital to the deserving and eligible units 
of MSME sector.  
(iii) Credit Guarantee Scheme for Micro and Small Enterprises (MSEs), for providing 
collateral free loan up to a limit of Rs. 200 lakh to MSEs with guarantee coverage 
up to 85 per cent  for various categories of loans. Further, Budget 2023 -24, has 
announced the infusion of Rs. 9,000 crore in the corpus of CGTMSE to enable 
additional credit of Rs. 2.00 lakh crore with a reduced cost of credit.   
(iv) New revised criteria for classification of MSMEs. 
(v) No global tenders for procurement up to Rs. 200 crore. 
(vi) “Udyam Registration” for MSMEs, for Ease of Doing Business w.e.f. 1.7.2020 
(vii) Launching of an online Portal “Ch ampions” in June, 2020 to cover many aspects 
of e-governance including grievance redress and handholding of MSMEs. 
(viii) Inclusion of Retail and Wholesale traders as MSMEs w.e.f. 2.7. 2021. 
(ix) Non-tax benefits extended for 3 years in case of an upward change in sta tus of 
MSMEs. 
(x) Launch of Udyam Assist Platform on 11.1.2023 to bring Informal Micro 
Enterprises (IMEs) under the formal ambit for availing the benefits under Priority 
Sector Lending.  
(xi) The Ministry of MSME  vide Notification no. S.O. 5670(E) dated 9.11.2018, had 
made it mandatory for all Central Government Ministries/Departments/ CPSEs to 
procure at least 25  per cent of their annual procurement from MSEs, including 3  
per cent from MSEs owned by women entrepreneurs vis-a-vis the target of 25 per 
cent, Central Public Sector Enterprises (CPSEs) procured 34  per cent from Micro 
& Small Enterprises in 2022-23.  
(xii) Field offices of Ministry of MSME organize various awareness campaigns for 
UDYAM registration  and benefits of Go vernment schemes /programmes, in 
coordination with MSME/ Industry Departments of States/UTs concerned and 
other MSME stakeholders through physical workshops, social media, print media 
& electronic media for creating wide publicity for increasing participat ion from 
all stake holders.  
(xiii) To address the issue of delayed payment to MSMEs, RBI has issued guidelines 
for setting up and operating the Trade Receivables Discounting System (TReDS) 
to facilitate the financing of trade receivables of MSMEs from corporate and 
other buyers, includ ing government departments and P ublic Sector Undertakings 
(PSUs) through multiple financiers electronically. 
  

5  
10. The Committee welcomes the goal of the Government for making India a $5 
trillion economy by the Year 2024-25 and opines that the target can be achieved by 
growth and development of the MSME sector. As MSME sector is vital for fostering 
entrepreneurship and generating self -employment opportunities at comparatively 
lower capital cost  and are complementary to large indu stries as ancillary units , 
formulation of targeted policies in the areas of infrastructure development, 
technological upgradation and forward linkage s could help MSMEs to achieve their 
full potential and propel the Indian economy to a higher growth traject ory. The 
Committee recommends that Government need to play a proactive role in promoting 
MSME Sector by handholding the MSME s at the grassroots level and for this , a top 
down approach needs to be implemented right  down to the last tier of the MSME 
sector in letter, spirit and action.  In this regard, a roadmap should be devised to 
achieve the desired results.

Inclusion; (ii) Access to f inance; (iii) Access to market ; (iv) Access to technology ; (v)

skilling/reskilling.

generating gainful employment and sustainable livelihoods; (iv) enhance servi ce sector 
through capacity  building/skilling; (v) gender parity in entrepreneurship; and (vi) ensure 
access to  markets and enhance MSMEs  share of exports.

Scheme of Fund for Regeneration of Traditional         Industries (SFURTI) 
48. SFURTI is a scheme implemented by the Ministry to organize traditional industries  
and artisans into clusters to make them competitive and provide support  for their long term 
sustainability, sustained employment, to enhance marketability of products of such clusters, 
to equip traditional artisans of the associated clusters with the improved skills, to make 
provision for common facilities and improved tools and equipment for artisans, to  
strengthen  the cluster governance systems with the active participation of the stakeholders, 
and to build up innovative products, improved technologies,  advanced processes, market 
intelligence and new models of public -private partnerships.  The Budget Estimates for the 
FY 2023-24 for the SFURTI Scheme is Rs. 280.00 crore. 
 
49. The Committee was informed by the Ministry that so far , 498 clusters have been 
approved and a pproximately Rs. 1292 crores assistance committed for these clusters 
covering about 2.94 lakh artisans . Out of the approved clusters, 275 clusters are operational 
and income of artisans has  increased by av erage 83 per cent  from pre -intervention level . 
Even, 203 clusters were made functional between the FYs 2020-22 despite the COVID-19 
disruptions. Besides, the Ministry has taken some new initiatives such  as, (i) f ocus on 
Aspirational and uncovered districts; (ii) participation of artisans in SPV management raised 
from 1/3rd to 2/3 rd; (iii) introduction of design experts, e -commerce, and renewable energy 
as part of Model Cluster ; and (iv) i mplementation of timeline of clusters has been reduced 
from 36 months to 18 months.

COIR BOARD/COIR VIKAS YOJNA 
 
53. The Coir Vikas Yojna  is implemented by the Coir Board which is a statutory body 
established under the Coir Industry Act, 1953 for promoting overall development of the coir 
industry and improving the living condition of the workers engaged in this traditional 
industry. The act ivities of the Board for development of coir industries, inter -alia, include 
undertaking scientific, technological and economic research and development activities , 
developing new products & designs; and marketing of coir and coir products in India and 
abroad.  It also promotes co -operative organizations among producers of husks, coir fibre, 
coir yarn and manufacturers of coir products; ensuring remunerative returns to producers 
and manufacturers, etc.  Coir Board is actively implementing the following schem es/ 
programmes for the sustainable development, growth and encouragement of coir artisans of 

24  
coir industry all over the country under the umbrella scheme Coir Vikas Yojna  which 
consists of the following components: 
• Science & Technology 
• Skill Upgradation and Mahila Coir Yojana 
• Domestic Market Promotion 
• Export Market Promotion 
• Trade & Industry Related Functional Support Services 
• Welfare Measures 
  
54. Under the Coir Vikas Yojna , various programmes like R and D activities, Market 
Development Programmes, Entrepreneurship Development Programme, Awareness 
Programme, Workshop, Seminar, Exposure Tour, etc. are organised under various 
components of the scheme for attracting more entrepreneurs to coir sector. In order to create 
skilled man power required for the  coir industry , the Board is organizing various training 
programmes on manu facture of value added products,  skill development and employment 
generation (through Skill Upgradation and Mahila Coir Yojana), providing assistance for 
setting up new units throug h PMEGP Schemes, and Welfare measures for coir workers. 
Assistance is provided for export and domestic market promotion in coir sector.  
 
55. The Committee sought response from the Ministry about the details of export 
performance of coir and coir products during the last three years and the efforts made by the

of Common Facility  Centers (CFCs) in the existing clusters and for establishment of new/ 
upgradation of existing Industrial Areas/Estates/Flatted Factory Complex. MSE-CDP is a

approved from 2021-22 to 2025 -26 with a budgetary support of Rs.1, 744.87 crore. In FY

been approved by the Ministry.

National Small Industries Corporation (NSIC) 
 
79. NSIC, a CPSE under the Ministry of MSME, has been given mandate of promoting, 
aiding and fostering the growth of the MSME s with blending of objectives of its operations 
into “Commercial” as well as “Promotional” activities. For fulfilling its mandate, NSIC 
provides integrated support to MSMEs under Marketing, Technology, Credit and other 
Support Services on commercial basis through a set of specially tailored schemes. NSIC 
plays the role of “facilitator” and complements various other institutions performing such 
activities in singularity.  The Committee was informed about t he Business Plan of NSIC 
which is as follows: 
 
• RAW MATERIAL DISTRIBUTION (RMD):  Facilitating the supply of Raw 
Material to MSMEs has been one of the important activities of NSIC. Key raw 
materials like Iron & Steel, Aluminum, Copper, Polymer, Bitumen, Emul sion, 
Cement etc. are facilitated from bulk producers by entering into MoUs with them. 
Major portion of the discounts received by NSIC from the bulk suppliers are passed 
on to the MSMEs to make their end product more competitive in the market.  
• Single Poin t registration Scheme (SPRS) : NSIC registers Micro and Small 
Enterprises (MSEs) under Single Point Registration Scheme (SPRS) for participation 
in tender floated by CPSEs. The units registered under SPRS of NSIC are eligible to 
get the benefits under Publi c Procurement Policy for Micro and Small Enterprises 
(MSEs) Order 2012. The projected number of units to be served is 28500 units 
for the financial year 2023-24. 
• Action Plan under Credit support (RMA, Bill Discounting & Bank Tie -up), 
2023-24: 
• Arrangements/MoUs with Government & Private bulk suppliers to provide 
the raw material to MSMEs at cheaper/competitive rates. 
• Providing financial assistance to MSMEs against the security of Bank 
Guarantee. 
• MoUs with leading Banks and FIs to provide more op tions to MSMEs to fulfil 
their credit needs. 

33  
• Wider penetration of schemes through various online and offline platforms i.e 
Marketing Campaigns, participation in Industry association programmes conducted 
by Assocham, PHD Chamber of Commerce & Industry, Lagh u Udyog Bharati, SME 
India, FICCI etc. 
• One-stop solution for MSMEs in getting them credit support from NSIC & 
Banks and provide them with raw material assistance.    
•  NSIC marketing portal (Business to Business): NSIC facilitates MSMEs to 
capture new markets through MSME Global Mart Web Portal msmemart.com. The 
portal provides an online platform to B2B (Business to Business) marketing 
activities, which has features like Inter active database of MSMEs, Global and 
National Tender Notices, Self -Web development tool, Centralized Mail System, 
Popular product section, Unlimited Global Trade Leads, Multiple Language Support, 
Discussion Board, Call centre support, Payment Gateway for membership. 
 
TECHNOLOGY: NSIC through its Technical Services Centres facilitates MSMEs 
by providing trained manpower and offers material testing facilities and common 
facility services. The demand driven – industries oriented training programme 
offered by N SIC caters to high -tech areas as well as conventional trades. Further, 
NSIC is continuously exploring to add industry -oriented demand driven 
skill/entrepreneurship development training programs in consultation of  local 
industry and other stakeholders. 
 
80. NSIC has been able to establish Livelihood Business Incubators (LBIs) at 8 locations 
namely Deoria, Naini, Nawada, Kashipur, Chennai, Rajkot, Neemka (Faridabad) and 
Rourkela and Incubation Centres at four locations namely, Okhla (New Delhi) , Howrah, 
Guwahati and Mandi. However, NSIC is continuously exploring the possibility to establish 
LBIs at other locations for which communications were sent to the State Governments 
requesting for providing built up space to house the LBIs. Communication to other 
Institutions/PSUs was also made seeking space for the LBI. NSIC has already established 
an LBI at Rourkela on the built up space provided by SAIL –Rourkela Steel Plant free of 
cost and the recurring expenditure is being extended by the National Scheduled Tribe 
Finance and Development Corporation under grant. 
 
81. The Committee was informed that various constraints are being faced by NSIC with 
regard to raw material acquisition from CPSEs and other sources viz. (i) NSIC has no 
special allocation of material from CP SEs for distribution among the MSMEs; (ii) t he 
material offered by CPSEs are often not in sync with the requirement of MSMEs ; (iii) n o 
credit facility is provided by CPSEs to NSIC fo r procurement of their material; and (iv) n o 

34  
special prices are offered by CPSEs to NSIC for the distribution of material among MSMEs. 
Besides, no financial support is provided by the Government to NSIC to acquire raw 
materials from CPSEs on credit  basis. NSIC has no control over the prices of raw materials 
as prices are decided  by the respective manufacturer of the material  and NSIC has been 
taking up the issues regularly with concerned Ministries and CPSEs.  
 
82. The Committee is of the view that one of the major constraints being faced by 
the MSMEs is the exorbitant price of raw materials at which they are provided by the 
National Small Industries Corporation ( NSIC) and, therefore, corrective measures 
should be taken for supplying the raw materials to MSMEs at affordable concessional 
rates so that the MSMEs could be able to survive in the domestic market as well as 
compete with their counterparts in the overseas market. Also, alternative options 
should be explored instead of becoming  solely dependent on NSIC to  fulfill the raw 
material requirements of MSMEs.   
 
83. NSIC provides training through Incubation Centres for the purpose of skill 
development and employment generation. The NSIC also offers the demand driven -
industries oriented training programme s which caters to high -tech areas as well as 
conventional trades.  The Committee recommends that NSIC should explore the 
possibility of establishing more Incubation Centres in order to impart training to the 
potential entrepreneurs/youth in the areas of business operation for their gainful 
employment. If need be, additional funds may be sought at the RE stage to  continue 
imparting more training t o the potential entrepreneurs/ youth/artisans with special 
focus on women artisans for the overall growth of the MSME Sector. 
 
84. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should analyze the various 
constraints being encountered by the NSIC with regard to acquisition of raw materials 
from CPSEs and other sources and take up the matter at the appropriate level with 
the concerned admi nistrative Ministries of CPSEs for special allocation of raw 
materials at reasonable/affordable prices for distribution among MSMEs, including 
extending credit facility to the NSIC for procurement of such raw materials.

Credit Support/Guarantee Schemes 
 
95. The Credit Support/Guarantee Scheme for MSMEs is a Government initiative 
designed to provide financial assistance to MSMEs. To implement the scheme, Credit 
Guarantee Fund Trust for Micro and Small Enterprises (CGTMSE) was jointly set up by 
Ministry of MSME and Small Industries Development Bank of India (SIDBI) to ensure 
flow of institutional credit to the Micro and Small Enterprises  (MSEs). Credit Guarantee 
Scheme (CGS) was launched to strengthen credit delivery system and to facilitate flow of 
credit to th e MSE sector. Through this scheme, the guarantee cover is provided for 
collateral free credit facility extended by Member Lending Institutions (MLIs) to the new as 
well as existing MS Es. The maximum loan limit has been enhanced from Rs. 100 lakh to 
Rs. 200 lakh and corpus of this fund has also been enhanced from Rs. 2500 crore to 7500 
crore.  
 
96. The Committee was apprised that scheme , which is administered by SIDBI,  provides 
access to credit from banks and other financial institutions to MSEs, and also pr ovides a 
guarantee to the lenders against default  which reduces the risk of lending to MSEs . Under 
the scheme, MSEs can avail of credit up to Rs. 5 crore with a repayment period of up to 5 
years. The scheme also  provides collateral-free loans, which means that the borrower does 
not need to provide any security or collateral to avail of the loan. The scheme is aimed at 
helping MSEs access to credit at competitive interest rates and also to reduce the risk of 
lending to MSEs. The scheme also helps MSEs to exp and their businesses and creation of 
new employment opportunities. The scheme is available to all the MSEs operating in the 
manufacturing, services or agricultural sectors. 
 
97. The CGTMSE has covered more than 67 lakh beneficiaries so far and t he 
beneficiaries have experienced a boost in their turnover as well as employment generation 
a f t e r  approval of CGTMSE funding. I t  h a s a positive impact on six major areas in the 
MSE sector, viz. technology  upgradation, skill upgradation, market development, 
sustainability of scheme, economic impact, and social impact. The scheme has been 
successful in spanning itself geographically across the country with a special focus in  the 
North East. The benefits of the scheme have also reached more than 100  industrial sectors 
in which MSEs are operating. The beneficiaries are not just limited to major industrial 
hubs but are also spread even in tier 3 towns.  CGTMSE has been highly effective in settling 
the claims wherein the first  installment was settled within one month in majority of the 
cases. Following are the eligibility criteria for credit guarantee under CGTMSE: 

40  
• New or existing Micro and Small Enterprises [MSEs] engaged in 
manufacturing, service, retail trade, wholesale trade & educational Institutions 
activities. 
• Collateral security and third party guarantee free credit facility up to Rs. 200 
lakh extended to the MSEs. 
• In the partial collateral security model, the MLIs are allowed to obtain 
collateral security for a part of the credit facility, whereas for the  remaining 
unsecured part of the credit facility, up to a maximum of Rs. 200 lakh, can be 
covered under Credit Guarantee Scheme of CGTMSE. 
• For the credit facilities extended by MLIs and covered under Credit Guarantee 
Scheme of CGTMSE, CGTMSE extends guaran tee coverage which ranges 
from 75% to 85  per cent  as applicable under the scheme depending on the 
category of the borrower and credit limit.  
• As on date, CGTMSE has 150 Member Lending Institutions (MLIs) including 
all Public-Sector Banks, some of Private S ector and Foreign Banks, NBFCs, 
State Financial Institutions, Small Finance Banks, RRBs, Co-operative Banks.

Fund of Funds (Self Reliant India Fund (SRI)   
130. The Committee was informed that the objective of Self Reliant India Fund (SRI 
Fund) is to address the  ever-unresolved needs of equity & capital of MSMEs. It is essential 
to identify pools  of capital which can be further leveraged in order to create a multiplier 
effect on the  economy and, therefore, making MSMEs more competitive in the global 
markets: 
 Under Atmnirbhar Bharat Package , the Government of India announced to set up  a 
Rs.10, 000 crore Fund of Fund s for MSMEs. This fund, which is called Self Reliant  
India (SRI) Fund, has the objective of supporting Venture Capital (VC)/Private Equity 
(PE) firms investing in the MSME sector to encourage them to invest in the MSME  
segment and will address the equity funding challenges of MSME sector and  give 
them a thrust to break their barriers, encourage corporatization and allow them  to grow 
to their full inherent potential to become global champions. With Government 
intervention, the Fund would be able to channelize diverse variety of funds into under -
served MSMEs and address the growth needs of viable and high growth MSMEs. 
 In order to implement the SRI Fund, on 1 st September, 2021, a Special Purpose  
Vehicle (SPV) viz. National Small Industry Corporation (NSIC) Venture Capital Fund  
Limited (NVCFL) got registered as an Alternative Investment Fund (AIF) Category -II. 
Subsequently, the Contribution Agreement amongst (i) Ministry of MSME, Government 
of India (ii) National Small Industries Corporation Limited (iii) NSI C Venture Capital 
Fund Limited (iv) SBI-CAP Ventures Limited was signed on 12th October, 2021. 
 The funds to be mobilised by the Daughter funds and funds to be committed by SRI

133. Fund of Funds, also called the Self Relian t India (SRI) Fund, has been 
formulated for addressing the equity funding challenges of MSME sector and  give 
them a thrust to break their barriers, encourage corporatization and allow them  to 
grow to their full potential to become global champions. It was observed by the 
Committee that the Actual Expenditure of Rs. 212.57 crore (up to 31.01.2023) has been 
utilized which is only 53.66 per cent of the RE allocation of Rs. 439.40 crore  for the 
FY2022-23. The Committee recommends that the remaining amount should be utilized

the FY2023-24 should be utilized optimally and evenly throughout the year.

augment the efforts of the Government in expanding and diversifying mobilisation of 
capital for MSME businesses. An increased capital pool will definitely help enterprises 
reach their full potential and become national/international champions. The 
Committee recommends that SRI  Fund should launch a technology platform to 
establish a transparent and standardized procedure for Daughter Funds to seek 
investments, which will also assist in compliance and reporting for statutory and 
administrative purposes. 
 
Studies, Publicity & International Cooperation (SPIC) 
135. The Committee was informed that th e Studies, Publicity & International Cooperation 
(SPIC) is formed by merging of schemes  like, International Cooperation Scheme, 
Information Education and Communication (IEC), Survey, Studies and Policy Research and 
National Award and National Board Schemes with the direction of M inistry of Finance. 
Now, the scheme has following sub components:  International Cooperation sub component 
aims to build capacity of MSMEs for entering export market by facilitating their 
participation in international exhibitions/fairs/conferences/seminar s/buyer-seller meets 
abroad as well as providing them with actionable market-intelligence and reimbursement of 
various costs involved in export of goods and services. Now, the three main activities in the 
revised International Cooperation  guidelines are Market Develo pment Assistance of 

51  
MSMEs (MDA);  Sub-Component Capacity Bui lding of First Time MSE Exporters 
(CBFTE); and Sub -Component 3 Framework for International Market Intelligence 
Dissemination (IMID).  
  
136. The objective of the scheme is to give wide publicity to the various schemes of the 
Ministry and office of DC(MSME) being run with the aim of providing financial assistance, 
technological assistance and upgradation, infrastructure development, skill develo pment and 
training and market assistance to MSMEs, etc.  
 
137. The main objectives of Survey, Studies and Policy Research  component are to 
periodically collect relevant and reliable data on various aspects and features of MSMEs, to 
study and analyze the c onstraints and challenges faced by the MSME as well as the 
opportunities available to them, in the context of liberalization and globalization of the 
economy and to use the results of these surveys, evaluation studies of scheme for th e 
Ministry and analyti cal studies for policy research, designing appropriate strategies and 
measures of intervention by the Government. Under the scheme, data on enterprises owned 
and/or managed by women, SC ST and OBC are also collected.  
 
138. The main objective of National Award and National Board component is to recognize 
the contributions of MSME entrepreneurs for their outstanding performance and motivate 
and encourage them. The Annual National Award started in the year 1983, when 19 
entrepreneurs were conferred awards. Th e last award was given on 30th June, 2022 wherein 
35 awards were conferred on MSMEs. 
 
139. The budget allocation for Studies, Publicity & International Cooperation (SPIC) for 
the FY2023-24 is Rs. 36.07 crore.  
 
140. It is learnt that performance of the MSMEs during the last five years has not 
been very encouraging.  The Committee recommends that a comprehensive study 
needs to be conducted by the Ministry of MSME to fathom the current situation of 
MSME sector in the co untry and to find out the exact impact of COVID -19 Pandemic 
on the MSME sector and to know whether the MSME sector has actually recovered 
from the pandemic effect or still reeling under the impacts of the Covid Pandemic. The 
Committee may also like to be a pprised about the findings of the study for its 
consideration considering the fact that a resilient and dynamic MSME Sector will be 
instrumental in realising the goal of Make in India  and Atma Nirbhar Bharat  (Self 
Reliant India).

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE 
 
1. The Committee is of the view that the  new classification of MSMEs would bring 
about positive changes in the MSME Sector including many benefits that will aid 
MSMEs to grow in size by attracting inv estments and would generate more 
employment opportunities. In this regard, in the deposition by the Secretary, Ministry 
of MSME on 20.02.2023 before the Committee, it emerged that although the change in 
definition of MSMEs is for their benefit, however, a study is required for sector -wise 
segregation of the MSMEs. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should 
carry out a study for sector -wise segregation of the MSMEs in order to ensure 
targeted distribution of budgetary allocations which would facilitat e development, 
expansion and growth of the MSME sector.      
(Para 8) 
 
2. The Committee welcomes the goal of the Government for making India a $5 
trillion economy by the Year 2024-25 and opines that the target can be achieved by 
growth and development of the MSME sector. As MSME sector is vital for fostering 
entrepreneurship and generating self -employment opportunities at comparatively 
lower capital cost  and are complementary to large industries as ancillary units , 
formulation of targeted policies in the areas  of infrastructure development, 
technological upgradation and forward linkage s could help MSMEs to achieve their 
full potential and propel the Indian economy to a higher growth trajectory. The 
Committee recommends that Government need to play a proactive role in promoting 
MSME Sector by handholding the MSMEs at the grassroots level and for this, a top 
down approach needs to be implemented right down to the last tier of the MSME 
sector in letter, spirit and action. In this regard, a roadmap should be devised  to 
achieve the desired results.  
(Para 10) 
 
3.  The Committee observes that in many sub -heads, nil expenditure was incurred 
and re-appropriation of funds was resorted to  at the revised estimates stage . Although 
the re -appropriation of  funds for some of the schemes were got approved through 
Standing Finance Committee (SFC) at the end of the financial year , but the funds 
remained unutilized.  The Committee is of the view that it is not a healthy sign and 
such practices should be avoided as far as possible in future. 
(Para 17) 
  

53  
4. It was observed that the allocations for the FY 2022-23 of the Ministry were 
either decreased or increased at the revised estimate stage, but the actual expenditure 
incurred is less than the Revised Estimate. The Committee is of the view that scheme-
wise estimation of fund requirements should be carried out  effectively and sincerely  
well in advance to ensure that budget allocations are utilized optimally. 
(Para 18) 
 
5. The Committee notes that for the FY 2 022-23, the Ministry was allocated Rs. 
21422.00 crore which was reduced to  Rs. 15628.71 at the RE Stage and the A ctual 
Expenditure up to the 31st January, 2023  stands at only Rs. 11112.01 crore which is 
71.1 per cent of the RE allocation. The Committee is of serious concern in this regard 
and would like to be apprised about the reasons for such low utilization of allocations. 
The Committee is of the view that the Ministry should take necessary steps to utilize 
the balance amount of 29 per cent during the remaining period of the financial year in 
consonance with the Financial Rules . The Ministry should henceforth  rationalize its 
expenditure throughout the year to avoid uneven spending during the last quarter of 
the financial year.  
(Para 19) 
 
6. The Committee notes that an allocation of Rs. 199.88  crore was made at RE 
stage for the SME Division for the FY 2022-23 and the Actual Expenditure up to the 
31st January, 2023 stands at Rs. 118.46 crore, which is only 59.26 per cent of the RE 
allocations. A s regards to ARI Division, the  RE for  t h e  F Y 2022-23 was Rs. 
3321.46 crore whereas the Actual Expenditure up to the 31 st January, 2023 is Rs. 
2664.31 crore, which is 80.21 per cent of the RE allocation. In  case of Office of 
DC-MSME also, the RE was Rs. 12152.37 crore and the Actual Expenditure up to the 
31st January, 2023 is only Rs. 8329.24 crore which clearly shows that the  DC-MSME 
could utilize only 68 per cent of the RE for FY 2022 -23. The Committee would like to 
be apprised about the reasons for such low utilization of the allocations made and 
suggests to the Ministry that a systematic expenditure pattern should be devised to 
streamline its expenditure in future.  
(Para 20) 
 
7. The Committee notes that the BE for FY2023 -24 is Rs. 22137.95 crore, which is 
a slight increase from the BE of Rs. 21,422 crore for the FY2022 -23. Out of this , an 
allocation of Rs.  14,100 crore has been earmarked for  the Guaranteed Emergency 
Credit Line Scheme (GE CL) and, only Rs. 8037.95 crore is left for various other 
schemes of the Ministry for the FY2023-24. In absence    of adequate funds, it would be 
difficult for the Ministry to implement its various schemes  effectively in the present 

54  
scenario when the country had undergone the problems of COVID-19 Pandemic which 
hit the MSME Sector badly. The Committee recommends that  the Ministry  should 
ask for enhanced allocation at the RE Stage for proper implementation of its  flagship 
Schemes with a view to strengthening the MSME Sector.  
(Para 21) 
 
8. Taking into consideration the views expressed by some of the MSME 
Associations, t he Committee is of the opinion  that the Ministry should w ork in close 
collaboration with various MSME Associations in order to address the difficulties 
being faced by them and provide a detailed note on the action taken thereon for 
consideration of the Committee.  Further, surveys, if any, conducted by any MSME 
Associations like Consortium of Indian Associations, should be considered for the  
benefit and growth of the MSME Sector and benefit of the artisans.  
(Para 23) 
 
 
9. The Committee notes that the Actual Expenditure up to 31.01.2023 in respect of 
important schemes under KVIC such as Khadi Vikas Yojana, Gramodyog Vikas 
Yojana,  Khadi Grant and PMEGP  are 71.88  per cent, 72.08  per cent , 86.68 per cent

of the view that  these schemes are essential for creating employment and livelihood 
opportunities  in rural areas and underutilization of funds would adversely affect the 
employment prospects in the  country and recommends that the Ministry should pla n 
its expenditure pattern in a systematic manner so that the funds allocated for the 
schemes implemented by KVIC are optimally utilized for employment generation and 
strengthening rural economy.  
(Para 30) 
 
10. The Committee is of the view that KVIC should focus more on its technology 
improvement/upgradation as well as products upgradation/design aspects in order to 
compete with other players operating in the domestic and overseas market.  The 
Committee recommends that effective training programmes by experienced and 
experts having expertise in the field should be imparted to the artisans through its 
network of training institutions for product design and quality improvement so that 
the target of export promotion of Khadi products and employment generation for the 
people/artisans is achieved. 
(Para 31) 
 
 
11. The Committee appreciat es the efforts being made b y KVIC in promoting 
Khadi and Village Industries for providing employment opportunities in the rural as 

55  
well as urban areas thereby strengthening the rural economy. KVIC touches the 
poorest of the poor by providing livelihood opportunities to them while keeping intact 
the skill and craftsmanship of the artisans. However, there is a need to put  more 
emphasis on creating awareness among the masses particularly youth, about the Khadi 
Institutions and the wide range of Khadi and Village Industries products for wider 
outreach as people are m ostly aware of Khadi outfits only. The Committee is of the

create awareness regarding Khadi products and handholding of artisans, traditiona l 
craftsman and above all potential women entrepreneurs who want to set up their own

modernize their existing outlets/emporiums as well as open new outlets to attract

regional languages, for  the artisans  through its network of training institutions on 
product design and quality improvement in  order to promote export of Khadi 
products. Expressing concern over the infringement of Khadi trademark by some 
entities by engaging in unauthorized sale of products i n the name of Khadi, the

check such type of infringements.

youth, traditional and prospective artisans through the establishment of micro -
enterprises; and facilitating the participation of financial institutions for encouraging

Region (NER) in  t h e  FY 2022-23 (up  to 10.02.2023)  was much  less vis-a-vis the 
employment generated in the FYs 2019-20, 2020 -21 and 2021 -22. Although the

progress made towards employment generation is not encouraging  under this

aspects of the Programme and devise a more systematic approach for its better output 
and handholding of potential entrepreneurs, including women and SC/ST 
entrepreneurs, for employment generation  in the NER.

15. The Committee appreciates the steps  taken by th e Ministry for the overall 
implementation of the PMEGP Scheme. The Committee is of the view that the 
Ministry should generate awareness regarding the  scheme through greater media 
publicity and workshops, awareness camps etc. , especially in regional languag es, in 
order to encourage the  youth and artisans, with special focus on women artisans, for 
employment generation.  
(Para 46)

under the Scheme, around 87.48  per cent of the total applications were forward ed to 
the banks, 39.17 per cent of the total applications were  rejected by the banks and only 
31.04 per cent of the applications got sanctioned by the banks.  The Committee desires 
to know the reasons for such high rejection rate of applications by the banks. Keeping 
in view such an important  scheme of the Ministry, the Committee recommends  that 
the Ministry should look into the matter afresh and take necessary steps to remove the 
impediments by sensitizing the Bank officials and simplify the procedure with 
minimal formalities so as to sanction the loan applications in a time bound manner with

Rs. 334.00  crore which was reduced drastically to Rs. 1.95 crore only at the RE Stage

was reduced to Rs. 1.95 crore and the Ministry concentrated in utilizing the unspent 
balance of Rs. 200.00 crore lying with different implementing and nodal agencies.  In

kept in banks and so the amount remained unutilized whereas in the new system the 

57  
money comes to the Central Nodal Agency (CNA) where the unspent balance is first 
collected and then depending upon the actual expenditure in the field, the money is 
released, thereby helping in disbursement of money. The Committee is of the view that 
the new system of accounting should be accessible to the beneficiary actually in need 
and a cle ar set of guidelines from the top to the bottom should be put in place for 
accessibility of the intended beneficiary.  The Committee appreciates th e BE of Rs.

artisans.

beneficial to millions of rural artisans in the country engaged in variety of fields, as it

country. O ut of the 498 approved clusters under SFURTI, only 275 clusters are 
operational so  far and, therefore, t he  Committee  recommends that the   process of

artisans.

as coir sector is a good source of employment  in rural economy of the country 
especially for women artisans.

scope for skill development. Therefore, training and up-skilling become imperative for 
the growth and proliferation of coir industry into the untested, non-traditional areas of

training and skill development in areas of technological innovations , should be 
organized for the artisans at field level at regular intervals to enhance their skill and 
output for overall development of the coir sector. 
(Para 59)

21.  Under the Domestic Market Promotion, the application of  coir products 
remains limited to the floor covering material and coir mattresses.  Therefore, there is 
ample scope to improve the marketability of coir products by blending the coir fibre 
with other natural fibres highlighting the  benefits of  eco-friendly products. The 
Committee is of the view that not much support  is available to the Coir Industry to 
expand business in the domestic market and  therefore, recommends that the 
Government should support the industry  in the needed direction  and a scheme to 
realize/improve the domestic market potential should be formulated at the earliest for 
benefit of the coir workers/entrepreneurs.  
(Para 60)

during the years 2020 -21 and 2021-22 as the targets were achieved by the Coir Board. 
Further, the Committee notes that Coir pith with export earnings of Rs 1,349.63 crore 
constitutes 49 per cent of the total  export of coir products and Coir fibre with export 
earnings of Rs 498.43 crore con stitutes 18    per cent of the total exports. After 2014 -15, 
the value generated    from the export of non -traditional coir and coir products 
overtakes the value generated from the  export of traditional coir and coir products. 
Export Market Promotion Scheme helps exporters in reaching out to overseas market 
and helps in getting  much-needed business deals to support the industry. Thus, the 
role of the Coir Board is increasing as a promoter and facilitator of the industry and 
its focus should be on facilitating market-oriented development of the coir sector . The 
Committee is of the view that Coir Board should explore reaching out to  overseas 
markets which are still out of the ambit of export destination. Possibility of displaying 
coir products at the Indian Mis sions abroad should also be explored in order to create 
demand for coir products in overseas markets. Coir Board should also support in 
establishing fibre/yarn bank for sourcing  quality raw material to facilitate making 
quality traditional as well as non -traditional coir products for expanding  export 
markets.

amount of 34.43 per cent  would be utilized during the remaining period of the FY

Training Programmes, specifically in regional languages, should be  organised for the 
SC/ST entrepreneurs so that the sub -target of 4 per cent procurement from MSEs 
owned by them could be achieved. Particularly, efforts should be made to encourage 
and handholding of Tribal entrepreneurs for their effective participation i n the Public 
Procurement Process. 
(Para 94) 
 
36. The Committee appreciates the enhancement of the corpus of credit 
support/guarantee fund from Rs. 2500 crore to Rs. 7500 crore which is a welcome step 
which would prove beneficial towards the strengthening a nd development of MSME 
Sector. The Committee notes that an enhanced BE have been projected for Credit 
Support Programme for the FY 2023-24 i.e. Rs. 500.08 crore vis-à-vis the allocation 
made at BE & RE stage during the FY2022 -23 and wants  to know how the Mi nistry 
plans to utilize the projected budget for implementing its Credit Support 
Programmes/Schemes. The Committee  recommends that the projected budget should 
be utilized optimally for providing credit facilities to the MSMEs which are always 
looking for the credit for sustainability and development of their businesses. 
(Para 99) 
 
37. The Committee is of the view that the procedure of availing the credit facility 
should be simplified by reducing the paperwork , including streamlining the 
application process and introducing online loan applications , and documentation 

63  
requirements for loan applications  should be in regional languages  so that MSMEs 
even in rural areas can easily avail the credit facility.  
(Para 100) 
 
38. The Committee feels that m any of the MSMEs struggle or fail due to lack of 
proper financial knowledge or accessibility to financial guidance essential for running 
their businesses. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should devise a system 
in order to facilitate the MSMEs to have the benefit of financial guidance free of cost 
or paying a nominal charge from a network of financial advisors  who have 
specialization in working of the MSMEs. 
(Para 101) 
 
39. The Committee recommends that the Ministry should explore the feasibility of 
enhancing the limit of collateral free loans under CGTMSE, either term loan or 
working capital loan from the existing Rs. 2 crore to Rs. 5 crore to MSEs, irrespective 
of their consti tution (Private Ltd ., Partnership and/or Proprietorship) provided all 
other criteria are fulfilled . Besides, the annual guarantee fee charged by banks on 
providing CGTMSE coverage should be revisited and, if feasible, be reduced 
substantially as the benefi t of such credit guarantee is primarily taken away by the 
banks. A framework may be devised for inclusion of the agricultural activity and Self -
Help Groups under the Scheme should be considered favorably for employment 
generation and benefit of the people. 
(Para 102) 
 
40. The Committee was given to understand that the overall credit gap in the 
MSME Sector is more than Rs. 15 lakh crore across all the schemes of MSMEs. The  
Committee recommends that a systematic plan should be devised by the Ministry to 
bridge the existing credit gap in the MSME Sector so that the MSMEs are benefited 
for their overall development. 
(Para 103) 
 
41. The Committee notes that the BE for the FY 2022 -23 was Rs. 20.00 crore which 
was reduced to Rs. 4.00 crore only at the RE s tage and the Actual Expenditure (up to 
31.01.2023) is zero.  However, an amount of Rs. 22.23 crore has been projected as BE 
for the FY 2023 -24. Considering such an important and crucial Scheme like the 
ASPIRE for innovative entrepreneurship and generating employment opportunities in 
agro-rural sector by skilling, up -skilling and re -skilling unemployed and existing self -

64  
employed/wage earners in new technology , the Committee recommends that more 
budgetary provisions should be made  for the scheme at the RE stage and the Ministry 
of Finance should be approached in this regard. 
(Para 108) 
 
42. As agro -rural sector plays a vital role in the Indian economy and, therefore, 
there is a need to promote agro -based enterprises in rural areas so as to creat e 
employment opportunities for the rural youth. In this regard, the Livelihood Business 
Incubator (LBI) is the entity which can play a vital role in skilling, up -skilling and re-
skilling of the unemployed youth in rural and underserved areas. The Committee  
recommends that the Ministry should take initiatives for establishing more LBIs by 
simplifying the technical and procedural formalities so that the problem of poverty 
and unemployment is addressed properly for creating job opportunities in agro -rural 
sector. Further, awareness camps should be organised in the rural areas to create 
awareness among rural youth regarding benefits of these LBIs  and other useful 
schemes implemented by the Ministry of MSME. 
(Para 109) 
 
43. The Committee notes that an allocation of Rs. 50.72 crore was made at BE/RE 
stage under the MSME Champions Scheme and the Actual Expenditure is Rs. 36.83 
crore (up to 31.01.2023) which is 76.61 per cent of BE/RE allocation for the FY 2022-23 
which is not encouraging in view of the  importance of the Scheme.   The Committee is 
of the view that the components of the  scheme are quite important and the major 
objective of the scheme is to modernize the processes of MSMEs in order to increase 
their competitiveness to facilitate their natio nal and global reach and excellence . 
However, the BE for the FY2023-24 is Rs. 52.72 crore which is marginally higher vis-à-
vis the BE allocation for FY2022 -23. The Committee recommends that the Ministry 
should demand more fund s at the RE stage  as innovatio n and manufacturing 
techniques are of critical importance for the MSME sector to remain competitive. 
(Para 113) 
 
44. As per the data provided by the Ministry , Rs. 723.00 crore was allocated for the 
FY2022-23 for the Raising and Accelerating MSME Performance (RAMP) Scheme 
which was reduced to Rs. 410.01 crore at the RE Stage. However, the actual 
expenditure is Rs. 129.71 crore (up to 31.01.2023) which is only 31.63 per cent of RE 
allocation.  The Committee is conce rned about the under utilization of such an 
important scheme which aims at improving  access of MSMEs to market, finance and 
technology upgradation by enhancing  the outreach of existing schemes of the Ministry 
and suggests that the remaining allocation should be utilized within specified period in 
consonance with the Financial Rules. As an amount of Rs. 1170.00 crore has been 

65  
proposed under this scheme for the FY2023 -24 which is a significant enhancement as 
compared to allocations made for the FY 2022-23, the Committee hopes that the 
allocated amount would be sufficient to support various interventions in Covid 
resilience and recovery initiatives for MSMEs.  
(Para 119) 
 
45. The Committee feels that b y encouraging innovation s and necessary 
technological inputs to make the  MSMEs competitive and self -sufficient, th e RAMP  
scheme can complement the Atma Nirbhar Bharat Mission by boosting exports, 
reducing imports  thereby promoting domestic manufacturing. In this direction,  the 
Committee suggests that t he Ministry should actively involve the Industry 
Associations representing the MSMEs in their policy -decision making process in order 
to build up a robust MSME eco system in the country.  
(Para 120) 
 
46. The Committee notes that an allocation of  Rs. 24.96 crore  was made for the 
Procurement and Marketing Support (PMS) Scheme for MSMEs for the FY2022 -23 
which was enhanced to Rs. 40 crore at the RE stage but the actual expenditure as on 
31.01.2023 was only Rs. 9.52 crore , i.e. 25 per cent of the RE allocation .  On the other 
hand, the projected BE for the FY 2023-24 is Rs. 96.35 crore, which is significantly 
higher than any previous BE and RE  allocation. While the Committee appreciates  the 
higher BE for the FY2023-24 for the PMS S cheme which would help significantly in 
development of MSME Sector of the country , t he Committee recommends that 
optimal and full utilization of the allocation should be ensured in order to make the 
Scheme efficacious. 
(Para 124) 
 
47. The Committee notes t hat introduction of Guaranteed Emergency Credit Line 
(GECL) Scheme was a welcome move by the Government to provide much -needed 
financial assistance to MSMEs affected by the COVID -19 Pandemic. However, the 
utilization of the allocated amount of Rs. 15000.00  crore for the FY2022-23, which was 
reduced to Rs. 10,500.00 crore at the RE Stage, is not very encouraging as the actual 
expenditure (as on 31.01.2023) is Rs. 7500.00 crore only (i.e. 72 per cent of the RE 
allocation). The Committee recommends that the Mi nistry should ensure that the 
allocated amount of Rs. 14,100.00 crore for the FY2023 -24 is optimally utilized for 
efficient implementation of the scheme so that the MSMEs which have suffered due to 
the Covid -19 Pandemic are benefitted and the off take of l oan is enhanced for their 
overall growth and development.   
(Para 128) 

66  
48. The Committee is of the view that the corpus of Rs. 7500.00 crore provided so 
far was over leveraged and nearly equal the committed guarantee payment which 
restricts the effective o peration of the Scheme and therefore, the Ministry should take 
up the matter with the Ministry of Finance for increasing the loan amount available 
under the GECL Scheme for MSMEs as it would help increase their accessibility to 
funds they need to run and e xpand their businesses. Further, a flexible repayment 
terms and conditions should be adopted to make the Scheme more attractive for the 
MSMEs as it would help them manage their cash flow better and reduce the burden of 
repayment. Besides, lack of awareness about the Scheme is one of the main reasons for 
its low off take and, therefore, the Committee recommends that all regional languages 
should be adopted as medium of propagation in order to create awareness about the 
scheme and increasing its outreach among the MSMEs so that more and more MSMEs 
are aware of its benefits.  
(Para 129) 
 
49. Fund of Funds, also called the Self Reliant India (SRI) Fund, has been 
formulated for addressing the equity funding challenges of MSME sector and  give 
them a thrust to brea k their barriers, encourage corporatization and allow them  to 
grow to their full potential to become global champions. It was observed by the 
Committee that the Actual Expenditure of Rs. 212.57 crore (up to 31.01.2023) has been 
utilized which is only 53.66 per cent of the RE allocation of Rs. 439.40 crore for the FY 
2022-23. The Committee recommends that the remaining amount should be utilized in 
consonance with the Financial Rules and the BE allocation of Rs. 575.00 crore for the 
FY 2023-24 should be utilized optimally and evenly throughout the year.  
                                     (Para 133) 
 
50. The Committee is of the view that the SRI Fund scheme is able to channelize 
diverse variety of funds into underserved MSMEs and address the growth needs of 
viable and high growth MSMEs.  The Committee hopes that the SRI Fund should 
augment the efforts of the Government in expanding and diversifying mobilisation of 
capital for MSME businesses. An increased capital pool will definitely help enterprises 
reach the ir full potential and become national/international champions. The 
Committee recommends that SRI Fund should launch a technology platform to 
establish a transparent and standardized procedure for Daughter Funds to seek 
investments, which will also assist i n compliance and reporting for statutory and 
administrative purposes. 
(Para 134) 
 

67  
51. It is learnt that performance of the MSMEs during the last five years has not 
been very encouraging.  The Committee recommends that a comprehensive study 
needs to be conducted by the Ministry of MSME to fathom the current situation of 
MSME sector in the co untry and to find out the exact impact of COVID -19 Pandemic 
on the MSME sector and to know whether the MSME sector has actually recovered 
from the pandemic effect or still reeling under the impacts of the Covid Pandemic. The 
Committee may also like to be a pprised about the findings of the study for its 
consideration considering the fact that a resilient and dynamic MSME Sector will be 
instrumental in realising the goal of Make in India  and Atma Nirbhar Bharat  (Self 
Reliant India). 
(Para 140)

REPORT              
 
India has a thriving Heavy Industry Sector that is an integral part of the economy. Heavy 
Industry in India comprises of the heavy engineerin g industry, machine tools industry, heavy 
electrical industry, industry machinery and auto-in dustry. These industries provide goods and 
services for almost all sectors of the economy. The se are involved in the production of goods that 
are critical for the infrastructure development of the country and have a considerable share in the 
total manufacturing capacity of the country. The Go vernment of India has launched various 
initiatives such as Atmanirbhar Bharat, National In frastructure Pipeline, and National Green 
Hydrogen Mission, etc.  that are expected to further boost demand for the heavy products. In the 
Union Budget 2023-24, the Government of India has p resented seven priority areas “ Saptarishi ” 
and put greater emphasis on Investment in Infrastru cture and Green growth. To give further 
impetus to green mobility, the Government has allocated Rs 5171.97 crore for the flagship Scheme 
of MHI- Scheme for Faster Adoption of Manufacturing  of EVs (FAME) and also put forth 
measures such as Viability Gap Funding for Battery Energy Storage System (BESS), Support to 
Central and State Governments for Scrappage of old Vehicles and ambulances, Custom duty 
exemption on import of specified capital goods and machinery required for manufacture of 
lithium-ion batteries etc.   
 
2. After the presentation of the Union Budget (2023 -24), the Demands for Grants (2023-24) 
of the Ministry of Heavy Industries were referred t o the Department-related Parliamentary 
Standing Committee on Industry for examination and report thereon. The Committee considered 
and examined the Demands for Grants (2023-24) of the Ministry of Heavy Industries in its meeting 
held on the 20 th  February, 2023 during which the Secretary, M/o Hea vy Industries and Officers of 
the Ministry gave power-point presentation on the Demands for Grants (2023-24) of the Ministry. 
 
Ministry of Heavy Industries (MHI) 
3. The Ministry promotes the development and growth  of three sectors i.e . Capital Goods, 
Automobile and Heavy Electrical Equipment in the Co untry; and administers 21 CPSEs and 4 
autonomous bodies. Out of 21 CPSEs, 16 CPSEs are op erational and remaining 5 are under 
closure. The CPSEs under the Ministry are engaged i n manufacturing, consultancy and contracting 
services. The Ministry also looks after the Machine Building Industry and caters to the requirement 
of equipment for Basic Industry such as Steel, Mini ng, Non-ferrous Metals, Power, Fertilizers, 
Refineries, Petrochemicals, Shipping, Paper, Cement , Sugar, etc . The Ministry also supports the 
development of range of Intermediate Engineering In dustry such as Castings, Forgings, Diesel 
Engines, Industrial Gears, and Gear-Boxes.  
 
4. The Ministry maintains a constant dialogue with various Industry Associations in the 
Capital Goods, Automobile and Heavy Electrical Equi pment Sector and encourages initiatives for 

2 
 
the growth of industry in these areas. The Ministry  also assists the industries in achieving their 
growth plans through policy support, and other inte rventions such as advocating rationalization of 
tariff, promoting technological collaboration, research & development activities etc . 
 
Vision and Mission of MHI 
5. The Secretary, the Ministry of Heavy Industries,  during the course of discussion in the 
meeting of the Committee on 20 
th  February, 2023 to consider the Demands for Grants (2023-24) of 
the Ministry informed about the Vision & Mission of the Ministry which is as under: 
Vision 
"To have globally competitive, green & technology-d riven heavy industry manufacturing 
sector, including automotive and capital good secto rs, which propels growth and job 
creation" 
Mission 
"To facilitate Auto, Heavy Electrical & Capital Goo ds Sectors to be globally competitive, 
growth oriented and profitable and to provide all n ecessary support to CPSEs to improve 
their overall performance". 
 
Overview of the Demands for Grants (2023-24)

Overview of the Automotive Industry  
18. The automotive industry is one of the key drive rs of the Indian economy. Since the 
liberalization of the sector in 1991 and allowing 1 00 per cent FDI through automatic route, Indian 
automobile sector has come a long way. In its writt en submission to the Committee, the Ministry 
informed that today, there is a presence of major g lobal auto manufacturers in the country. All 
categories of vehicles like two-wheelers, three wheelers, passenger cars, light commercial vehicles, 
trucks, buses, tractors, heavy commercial vehicles,  etc. are produced in India and that India is the 

8 
 
second largest manufacturer of 2-Wheelers, the larg est manufacturer of 3-Wheelers and the 3rd 
largest manufacturer of passenger cars in the world. The Ministry further stated that manufacturing 
of automobiles including trucks, buses, cars, three  wheelers/ two wheelers etc . in India has risen at 
a very high pace. The industry produced about 22.9 million vehicles including Passenger Vehicles, 
Commercial Vehicles, Three Wheelers, Two Wheelers a nd Quadricycles in financial year 2021-22 
and about 19.8 million vehicles have been produced during the months of April to December 2022. 
 
19. As regards the industry’s domestic automobile s ales for Passenger Vehicles, Commercial 
Vehicles, Three Wheelers, Two Wheelers and Quadricycles, the Ministry submitted that the sale in 
financial year 2021-22 was 17.5 million and 16 mill ion for April  to December 2022. The Ministry 
also apprised the Committee that the Indian auto co mponent industry, with a well evolved 
manufacturing ecosystem, produces a wide variety of  products including engine parts, drive 
transmission and steering parts, body and chassis, suspension and braking parts, equipment and 
electrical parts, besides others to service the dyn amic automobile industry. According to the 
National Skill Development Corporation (NSDC), the auto industry provides direct employment to 
over 42 lakh people and indirect employment to 2.65  crore people. The automotive industry 
contributes 6% to India’s GDP and 35% to Manufacturing GDP. 
 
20. The Committee notes that the passenger car sect or of India grew significantly as India 
became the 3 
rd  largest manufacturer of passenger cars in the worl d.  At the same time, in 2-
Wheeler sector, India has slipped to 2 nd  position from the 1 st  position as compared to the 
FY2021-22. While the Committee commends the efforts  of the Ministry in respect of 
manufacture of passenger cars, it however notes wit h concern the decline in manufacturing 
of 2-Wheelers in view of the extensive use of 2-Whe elers in the country. The Committee is of 
the view that the Ministry should conduct a holisti c study and look into the shortcomings 
that have caused India to slip down to 2 nd  position in manufacturing of 2-Wheelers so that 
corrective measures can be taken timely to enable India to regain its position. 
 
Agricultural Machinery & Tractor Sector 
21.  Agricultural Machinery mainly consists of Agri cultural Tractors, Power Tillers, Combine 
Harvesters and other Agriculture Machineries & Impl ements. In its reply, the Ministry informed 
the Committee that due to negligible production of Power Tillers, Combine Harvesters and other 
Agricultural Machineries, this sector is mainly dom inated by Agricultural Tractors. Indian Tractor 
Industry is the largest in the world (excluding sub  20 HP belt driven tractors used in China), 
accounting for one third of the global production. The other tractor markets in the world are China 
and the United States. 
 
22. The Ministry also informed that Indian Tractors  were exported to US and other countries 
like Malaysia, Turkey, etc. Indian players have agg ressively started exporting to African countries 

9 
 
by bidding for government tender requirement. As su ch, Indian tractors are gaining acceptance in 
international markets. As the cost of tractors in I ndia is cheapest in the world, there is tremendous 
scope for improvement of export of tractors in future. 
 
23.  The Committee expresses its appreciation that Indian Tractor Industry has begun to 
make penetration slowly into the international mark et which is encouraging and laudable. 
However, it observes with concern that the producti on of Power Tillers, Combine Harvesters 
and other Agricultural Machineries are negligible a nd therefore recommends that the 
Ministry of Heavy Industries in coordination with t he Ministry of Agriculture and Farmers 
Welfare should work towards promotion of agricultur al tools and machinery which will 
ultimately boost the Agricultural Machinery Sector.  It is of the firm confidence that a robust 
push towards production of agricultural machineries  will go a long way in agriculture 
production of the country as well as bring in more revenue to the farmers. 
 
Electric Vehicles: Faster Adoption & Manufacturing of Electric (& Hybrid) Vehicles in India 
(FAME-India) Scheme 
 
24. Electric vehicles have been making headlines fo r decades. But it is only in recent years that 
EVs have been attracting seminal interest, innovation, and investments. Significantly, India has the 
world’s third-highest CO 2 emissions and the Government is advocating that em bracing EVs will 
help in reducing CO 2 and curbing air pollution. 
 
25. During the presentation on the Demands for Gran ts (2023-24) of the Ministry before the 
Committee, the Secretary of MHI stated that to redu ce dependency on fossil fuel and to address 
issues of vehicular emissions, the Government appro ved the scheme titled 'Faster Adoption and 
Manufacturing of Electric (&Hybrid) Vehicles in India' (FAME India) in March, 2015 for a period 
of 2 years w.e.f. 1
st  April, 2015. The Phase-I of FAME India Scheme has been extended from time 
to time till 31 March, 2019 with enhancement of tot al outlay to Rs. 895 crore. The Scheme had 
four focus areas i.e.  Technology Development, Demand Creation, Pilot Pro ject and Charging 
Infrastructure and it was successful in terms of cr eating the major policy discourse in Electric 
Mobility among all stakeholders including different  Departments of the Government of India and 
State Governments. 
26. The Secretary, MHI, further informed that, base d on the experience gained during Phase 1 
of FAME Scheme and suggestions of various stakehold ers, the Ministry notified Phase-II of the 
Scheme on the 8
th  March, 2019 for a period of 5 years, commencing fr om 1st April 2019, with an 
outlay of Rs. 10,000 crore. The main objective of t he scheme is to encourage faster adoption of 
Electric and Hybrid vehicles by way of offering upf ront incentive on purchase of Electric vehicles 
and also by establishing the necessary charging Inf rastructure required for electric vehicles. The 
scheme will help address the issues of environmenta l pollution and fuel security. In this phase of 

10 
 
the Scheme, more emphasis is given on electrificati on of public transportation that includes shared 
transport.

Safety of Electric Vehicles 
 54.  During the course of deliberations in the mee ting on the 20 
th  February, 2023, the 
Committee raised its concerns about incidents of fi re in the Electric Vehicles and suggested 

18 
 
installation of adequate safety measures in the Ele ctric Vehicles like fire extinguishing system in 
case of fire. The Ministry apprised the Committee t hat Ministry of Road, Transport and Highways 
looks after the safety aspect of the Electric Vehic les and that an expert committee has also been 
constituted and the committee has also given a repo rt. The Ministry informed the Committee that 
manufacturing guidelines for Electric Vehicles have  also been changed and after following these 
guidelines, there is less likelihood of such fire incidents taking place in the Electric Vehicles.  
 
55.  The Committee notes that the incidents of fire in E lectric Vehicles is a cause of concern 
and needs to be addressed properly. Most of the fir e catching incidents takes place in EVs when 
battery is damaged or punctured.  Apart from technical faults and manufacturing defec ts of 
batteries, many of the fire catching incidents may also be attributed to personal negligence of users 
by not taking proper precautions . The Committee recommends that the Ministry should  in 
consultation with the stakeholders analyse and asce rtain the root cause of fire incidents in 
EVs and find a solution for it so that such inciden ts do not take place so as to avoid any 
casualty. Besides, proper guidelines should be issu ed for the users and adequate awareness 
should be generated among the people regarding the proper usage of Electric Vehicles.  
 
56. The Committee recommends that adequate and inte rnationally accepted safety 
standards should be adopted to ensure safety of the  vehicles and its users. A proper venting 
mechanism for overheated cells in the battery must be put in place. Besides, the following 
safety measures to prevent fire hazards in the Electric Vehicles may be followed:  
(i) Use of fire-resistant materials such as aluminum, stainless steel, and other non-
combustible materials for the body of the electric vehicles.  
(ii) Use of fire-resistant insulation materials in the b attery compartment and other 
areas where the electric vehicle components are located.  
(iii) Installation of fire-extinguisher system in the bat tery compartment to 
extinguish any fires that may occur. 
(iv) Installation of fire-resistant wiring and other ele ctrical components to reduce 
the risk of fire due to short circuits.  
(v) Installation of fire-resistant brakes and other saf ety components to reduce the 
risk of fire due to friction.  
(vi) Installation of temperature sensors in the battery compartment to detect any 
overheating and activate the fire suppression system.  
(vii) Installation of battery management system to monito r the temperature and 
charge levels of the battery and alert the driver if any anomalies are detected.  
(viii) Installation of cooling system in the battery compa rtment to keep the 
temperature of the battery within a safe range.

57. As per the information furnished by the Ministr y, the “ Capital Goods " means any plant, 
machinery, equipment or accessories required for ma nufacture or production, either directly or 
indirectly, of goods or for rendering services, inc luding those required for replacement, 
modernization, technological upgradation or expansion. It contributes about 1.9 % to GDP.  
 
58.  The major sub-sectors of the Capital Goods Sector are as follows:

• Dies, Moulds and Press Tools 
• Plastic Machinery 
• Earthmoving and Mining Machinery 
• Metallurgical Machinery 
• Textile Machinery 
• Process Plant Equipment 
• Printing Machinery 
• Food Processing Machinery 
• Heavy Electrical equipment 
 
59.  Capital Goods Sector is crucial for the develo pment of the country’s economy because 
Capital Goods are considered essential for the development of domestic manufacturing capabilities 
from a national self-reliance perspective and Capit al Goods sector through a multiplier effect has a 
strong bearing on the growth and employment generat ion in the user industries as it provides 
critical inputs, i.e.  machinery and equipment for the entire manufacturi ng sector and other related 
sectors.

RECOMMENDATIONS/OBSERVATIONS OF THE COMMITTEE AT A GLANCE 
 
1. The Committee notes that the Budgetary allocation o f Rs 6171.63 crore for the 
Financial Year 2023-24 is the highest ever enhancem ent in comparison to the BE of the 
previous years. The Committee notes the significant enhanced fund allocation to the Ministry 
and hopes that the allocation would be utilized eff ectively in achieving the targets set by the 
Ministry for the Financial Year 2023-24. 
 (Para 7) 
 
2. The Committee also notes that the Ministry has been  able to utilize more than 99% of 
the funds provided at the RE Stage in the previous two Financial Years i.e.  2020-21 & 2021-
22. However, in the Financial Year 2022-23, the Min istry has been able to utilize only Rs. 
1428.71 crore, which is 44.36% of the RE allocation s of Rs. 3220.33 crore till 31.01.2023. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry should ensur e that the entire fund allocated at the 
RE stage is utilized effectively in consonance with  the financial policy and henceforth should 
rationalize the expenditure throughout the year eve nly to avoid any uneven spending during 
the last quarter of the financial year in future. 
 (Para 8) 
 
3. The Committee observes that the expenditure of the Ministry under most of its minor 
heads was sluggish throughout the Financial Year 20 22-23, and even at the fag end of the 
financial year, expenditure under “ Revenue Section ” was barely 43.6% of the RE and most 
of the funds under “ Capital Section ” was surrendered at the RE stage, which reflects 
imprudent financial management and planning. The Co mmittee recommends that the 
Ministry should draw up a clear and comprehensible plan for the Financial Year 2023-24 so 
as to avoid accumulation of the unspent funds in th e last quarter of the financial year and 
refrain from spending more than 33% of the allocate d amount during the last quarter of the 
financial year contrary to the General Financial Rules.  
(Para 10) 
4. The Committee observes that for the Financial Year 2023-24, the Budget Projection of 
the Ministry was Rs 6574.93 crore against which Min istry of Finance has allocated Rs 
6171.63 crore, which is about 93.87% of the project ion, as such, there is a shortfall of Rs 
403.30 crore in allocation. The budgetary allocatio n for the major Schemes of Ministry such 
as FAME India and Scheme for Competitiveness in Cap ital Goods Sector have also shortfall 
in allocation for the FY2023-24. The Committee reco mmends that the Ministry should take 
all-out effort to strategize and utilize the major part of the allocations timely and if need be,

effective implementation of these Flagship Schemes.
