5.19 The Committee observes that export promotion efforts have contributed to 
maintaining India‘s leadership position in global coir trade, with major markets including the 
United States, China, and European countries. However, emerging global trade uncertainti es, 

62 
 
including tariff and non-tariff barriers in key markets such as the United States, pose potential 
risks to export -dependent MSME sectors, including coir. Recent developments indicate that 
higher tariffs on Indian goods could adversely affect competitiv eness and export earnings of 
small producers. The Committee is concerned that the coir sector, dominated by micro 
enterprises with limited financial resilience, may face disproportionate impact from such 
external shocks. 
5.20 The Committee therefore, recom mends that the Ministry formulate a targeted 
export resilience strategy for the coir sector, including market diversification beyond 
traditional destinations, support for compliance with international standards, and 
financial risk -mitigation measures for M SME exporters. The Ministry may also 
coordinate with the Ministry of Commerce to proactively address tariff -related 
challenges through trade negotiations and export incentive frameworks. 
NATIONAL SMALL INDUSTRIES CORPORATION (NSIC) 
5.21     The National Small Industries Corporation Ltd. (NSIC), a Government of India 
enterprise under the Ministry of Micro, Small and Medium Enterprises, has been a key 
institutional pillar in the promotion and development of Micro, Small and Medium 
Enterprises across the cou ntry. The Corporation has been entrusted with the mandate of 
providing integrated support services in the areas of marketing, finance, technology and skill 
development, with a particular focus on enhancing MSME competitiveness, facilitating 
access to publi c procurement and fostering entrepreneurship among socially and 
economically disadvantaged groups. 
5.22     NSIC operates through an extensive nationwide institutional network comprising 101 
field offices, including 15 National SC/ST Hub Offices (NSSHOs), along with multiple 
Technical Service Centres and training -cum-incubation facilities. Through this network, 
NSIC delivers a range of services aimed at addressing critical constraints faced by MSMEs, 
particularly those relating to market access, technology adoption and capacity building. 
5.23     The Corporation provides integrated services through its field offices and eight 
National Technical Service Centres (NTSCs). Its major interventions include raw material 
distribution, credit facilitation and bill discounting, Single Point Registration for participation 
in Government procurement, and digital market access through the MSME Global Mart 
platform. During the year 2025, NSIC distributed 3, 64,374.60 metric tonnes of raw materials 
valued at ₹3,089.13 crore, indicating sustained demand for its input -support services. The 
MSME Global Mart platform onboarded 10,905 MSMEs during the year, thereby expanding 
digital market access for small enterprises. NSIC has also placed significant emphasis on skill 
development and technology transfer through its NTSCs, training 86,098 trainees in 2025 and 
providing MSMEs access to advanced manufacturing technologies such as CNC machining, 
CAD/CAM, 3D printing and emergin g applications in artificial intelligence and machine 
learning. 

63 
 
5.24     In furtherance of national priorities on social inclusion and equitable growth, NSIC 
implements the National SC/ST Hub (NSSH) Scheme, launched in 2016 to empower SC/ST 
entrepreneurs t hrough capacity building, market linkage and facilitation of participation in 
public procurement. NSIC also plays a central role in facilitating equity funding for 
high-potential MSMEs under the Self Reliant India (SRI) Fund, a ₹50,000 crore Fund of 
Funds initiative leveraging Government and private capital. Equity support under the SRI 
Fund is being channeled through 69 empanelled Daughter Funds under NSIC Venture Capital 
Fund Limited (as of October 2025). The Committee notes that NSIC‘s investment facilit ation 
activities are managed entirely through Internal and Extra -Budgetary Resources (IEBR), 
reflecting the Corporation‘s financial stability and operational maturity. During FY 2024 -25, 
NSIC recorded revenue of ₹3,431 crore, profit after tax (PAT) of ₹146 .30 crore (up 15.6% 
YoY) and paid its highest -ever dividend of ₹43.89 crore to the Government. The recent 
upgradation of NSIC from Schedule ‗B‘ to Schedule ‗A‘ Central Public Sector Enterprise 
(announced February 2026) further underscores its strategic imp ortance within the MSME 
ecosystem. 
5.25     The Committee notes that NSIC has demonstrated strong institutional capacity 
and operational performance through its nationwide network, integrated service 
delivery model and consistent financial results. However , the Committee is of the 
considered view that the scale of financing and growth capital required by the MSME 
sector—particularly for first -generation entrepreneurs, technology -intensive 
enterprises, export-oriented units and enterprises located in aspirational or underserved 
regions—far exceeds the present resource envelope available with NSIC. The 
Committee observes that the absence of a dedicated, large -scale growth financing 
mechanism significantly constrains the Corporation‘s ability to catalyse privat e 
investment and support MSMEs in scaling up operations, thereby limiting its potential 
developmental impact. 
5.26 The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry of MSME, in 
consultation with the Ministry of Finance, operationalise the pro posed ₹10,000 crore 
SME Growth Fund under NSIC in a phased, multi‑year manner, with a clearly defined 
implementation framework, timelines and measurable outcome parameters. The 
Committee emphasises that the proposed Growth Fund should be structured as a 
professionally managed vehicle, distinct from existing credit and guarantee schemes, 
and should focus on providing growth‑stage financing through blended‑finance, 
risk‑sharing and co‑lending models in partnership with financial institutions. Priority 
should be accorded to MSMEs engaged in technology upgradation, export‑oriented 
activities and enterprises operating in underserved and aspirational regions. 
5.27     The Committee further recommends that robust governance mechanisms be 
institutionalised for the p roposed Growth Fund, including the establishment of an 
independent investment committee, transparent eligibility criteria, periodic public 
disclosure of fund utilisation and outcome‑based monitoring linked to employment 
generation, enterprise growth and ma rket access. A mid‑term evaluation framework 

64 
 
should also be incorporated to enable timely course correction and ensure that the Fund 
contributes meaningfully to scaling MSME competitiveness and long‑term 
sustainability, while remaining consistent with the overall fiscal consolidation path. 
5.28     The Committee also observes that despite NSIC‘s expanded mandate, upgraded 
Schedule ‗A‘ status and commendable financial performance, its existing equity base of 
approximately ₹532 crore remains modest relative t o the scale of operations and 
financial support expected from the Corporation. The Committee notes that this limited 
capital base constrains NSIC‘s leverage capacity and necessitates greater reliance on 
borrowings from banks and financial institutions, oft en at higher costs, which 
ultimately affects the affordability of assistance extended to MSMEs. 
5.29     Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Ministry consider substantial 
equity infusion into NSIC  at the earliest to strengthen its capital base i n line with its 
strategic importance and enhanced responsibilities. The Committee is of the view that 
enhanced equity support would reduce dependence on high -cost borrowings, improve 
internal resource generation, and enable NSIC to offer more competitive i nterest rates, 
lower service charges and affordable support to MSMEs. 
5.30     The Committee further recommends that any equity infusion into NSIC be 
explicitly linked to measurable expansion in MSME coverage, particularly in priority 
sectors and underserv ed regions, so that the intervention directly translates into lower 
cost of finance, improved credit accessibility and sustainable scaling of NSIC 
operations, in alignment with national objectives such as Atmanirbhar Bharat and 
Viksit Bharat. 
MAHATMA GANDHI INSTITUTE FOR RURAL INDUSTRIALISATION (MGIRI) 
5.31 The MGIRI promotes sustainable rural industrialisation through science, technology 
and innovation, with roots tracing back to the All India Village Industries Association (1934) 
and the Jamnalal Bajaj Ce ntral Research Institute. Operating through six specialised 
divisions, MGIRI undertakes applied research, pilot studies, technology development, quality 
testing and capacity building to strengthen the Khadi and Village Industries sector, empower 
traditional artisans, and promote locally suited, resource -efficient technologies, thereby 
serving as a key technology support institution for rural enterprises. 
5.32 MGIRI has developed nine new products and seven machines/processes tailored to 
the needs of rural e nterprises, focusing on resource efficiency, renewable energy and value 
addition. It has also provided quality testing and technical guidance services to 61 agencies, 
including entrepreneurs, farmers and institutions, to ensure compliance with Indian stand ards 
and improve product quality. In addition, MGIRI has organised two major national -level 
workshops in collaboration with institutes of national importance to promote dissemination of 
its technologies and encourage stakeholder engagement in rural industrialisation.

CHAPTER 2: OVERVIEW OF BUDGETARY ALLOCATIONS AND 
SYSTEMIC ISSUES 
BUDGET ANNOUNCEMENTS OF 2025-26 AND IMPLEMENTATION STATUS 
1. The Committee notes with serious concern that while out of eight Budget 
announcements, only two — both led by the Ministry of MSME itself — have been 
operationalised. The remaining six, where the Ministry is a supporting agency, continue 
to languish at the stage of draft guidelines, inter -ministerial consultations, or 
preliminary deliberations without clearly defined or publicly disclosed rollout timelines. 
This pattern raises fundamental questions about the effectiveness of inter -ministerial 
coordination mechanisms and the Ministry's ability to influence outcomes where it is 
not the lead agency.  (Para-2.2) 
 
2. The Committee further observes that two announcements of particular 
significance to the MSME ecosystem — credit cards for micro enterprises and the 
scheme for first -time entrepreneurs (women and SC/ST) — remain unimplemente d 
nearly twelve months after their announcement. The credit card initiative, intended to 
reach ten lakh micro enterprises in the first year, has not progressed beyond the draft 
stage. The first-time entrepreneur scheme, which carries important equity and inclusion 
objectives, remains at the EFC memorandum stage. Taken together, these delays 
indicate a serious disconnect between the policy intent articulated in the Budget speech 
and the administrative machinery required for last-mile delivery. (Para-2.3) 
 
3. In view of the above, the Committee strongly recommends that a time -bound 
implementation framework be put in place for all Budget announcements concerning 
the MSME ecosystem, irrespective of whether the Ministry of MSME is the lead or a 
supporting Ministry. In particular, for the credit card scheme for micro enterprises and 
the term -loan scheme for first -time women and SC/ST entrepreneurs, the Committee 
urges the concerned Ministries to work in close coordination to finalise scheme design, 
obtain requisite ap provals and operationalise these initiatives within a clearly defined 
outer limit, preferably not later than the first half of FY 2026 -27. The Committee 
further recommends that progress on all eight announcements be monitored through a 
quarterly, inter‑min isterial review mechanism, anchored by the nodal 
Ministries/Departments concerned with active participation of the Ministry of MSME, 
with milestones, responsible agencies and timelines clearly specified. A consolidated 
implementation status be compiled and  shared with the Committee at regular intervals 
so that the credibility of Budget announcements is reinforced by demonstrable, 
time‑bound outcomes on the ground. (Para-2.4) 
 
4. The Committee notes with serious concern that out of the 7.61 crore MSMEs 
registered on the Udyam portal [including Informal Micro Enterprises on Udyam Assist 

67 
 
Platform (UAP) as on 31 January 2026], an overwhelming 7.56 crore (99.3%) fall under 
the micro category, while only about 4.88 lakh are classified as small and approximately 
36,816 as medium enterprises. This highly skewed distribution clearly indicates that a 
vast majority of enterprises operate at extremely small scales and are likely to have 
significantly different financial capacities, risk profiles, and support requirements 
compared to relatively larger micro units. (Para-2.6) 
 
5. The Committee reiterates that the upward revision of investment and turnover 
limits has the unintended consequence of all owing comparatively larger enterprises to 
remain within the micro segment, thereby risking dilution of the original intent of the 
MSME framework and constraining access to benefits for genuinely small and 
household-level enterprises. (Para-2.7) 
 
6. The Committee recalls that in its 327 th Report it had specifically recommended 
rationalisation of the MSME definitions and the creation of a separate Nano enterprise  
category; however, no tangible action has been taken by the Ministry so far. The 
Committee finds this inaction particularly concerning in light of emerging evidence and 
policy developments. In this regard, the Committee notes that the approach 
recommended by it has already been operationalised by the Government of Kerala, 
which has recognised Nano Enterprises as a distinct segment for units with investment 
up to ₹10 lakh and has introduced targeted schemes such as interest subvention, margin 
money assistance, and household enterprise promotion to address the specific needs of 
ultra-small entrepreneu rs. This State -level experience demonstrates both the 
administrative feasibility and developmental necessity of such differentiation. (Para-2.8) 
 
7. In view of the foregoing, the Committee strongly reiterates its earlier 
recommendation and urges the Ministry to undertake, without further delay, a 
comprehensive review of the MSME classification framework and introduce a separate 
Nano enterprise category with an appropriate threshold around ₹10 lakh investment. 
The Committee expects the Ministry to furnish a con crete and time-bound action plan, 
along with an assessment of the likely impact on credit access, employment generation, 
and inclusion, so as to ensure that policy support reaches the most vulnerable and 
genuinely small enterprises. (Para-2.9) 
 
8. The Committee also observes serious delays in the operationalisation of 
inclusion- and employment -oriented Budget announcements, particularly the scheme 
for first -time entrepreneurs for women and SC/ST beneficiaries and the proposed 
logistics and service deliv ery support to MSMEs through India Post. These 
announcements continue to remain under inter -ministerial consultation without clearly 
defined or publicly disclosed rollout timelines. (Para-2.11) 
 
 
 
 

68 
 
9. The Committee therefore recommends: 
 
a. All pending MSME -related Budget announcements be operationalised within a 
clearly defined and publicly notified timeline, not exceeding six months from the 
date of the Budget presentation. 
b. The Ministry be formally designated as the nodal authority for all MSME credit-
related Budget announcements and be empowered to enforce bank -level 
accountability. 
c. The Ministry should mandate written reasons for rejection of MSME loan 
applications covered under credit gua rantee schemes, prescribe time -bound 
grievance redressal mechanisms, and recommend penal action against lending 
institutions for repeated non-compliance. 
d. No MSME credit scheme be approved or reported as "implemented" unless it 
incorporates mandatory compon ents for technology upgradation, market 
linkage, and enterprise capability enhancement. (Para-2.13) 
 
IMPACT OF US TARIFFS ON MSME SECTOR 
 
10. The Committee, accordingly, strongly recommends: 
 
a. The Government intensify  efforts to diversify export destinations for MSME 
products to reduce over -dependence on a few major markets and minimise 
concentration risk. 
b. Establishment of a dedicated MSME Trade Defence and Support Mechanism to 
provide legal, technical and advisory ass istance in dealing with foreign tariff 
actions and trade-remedy investigations. 
c. Design and operationalise an MSME Tariff Resilience Package within RAMP 
and PMS, with components for targeted working -capital support, subsidised 
testing/certification/quality upgradation, and dedicated support for market 
diversification towards EU, ASEAN, West Asia and Africa. 
d. Creation of targeted contingency credit lines or interest subvention mechanisms 
for MSMEs in affected clusters facing immediate financial stress from sud den 
tariff changes. 
e. Development of an early -warning and real -time monitoring system to track 
global trade policy developments impacting MSMEs, enabling proactive policy 
intervention. 
f. Structured inter -ministerial coordination among the Ministries of Commerc e, 
MSME, Textiles and Finance be institutionalised to ensure a unified, timely and 
effective response to future external trade disruptions. (Para-2.18) 
 
 

69 
 
QUARTERLY EXPENDITURE PLAN (QEP) ANALYSIS OF LAST THREE 
FINANCIAL YEARS 
11. The Committee therefore recommends: 
 
a. QEP and MEP be adhered to, outcome-oriented planning instruments and not as 
procedural formalities. 
b. The Ministry institutionalise  contingency-based QEP planning to address 
predictable disruptions such as elections, ensure completion of all major 
administrative and financial approvals within the first quarter, and 
operationalise a substantial portion of budgeted expenditure within th e first 
three quarters. 
c. Persistent concentration of expenditure in the final quarter should be specifically 
explained to Parliament. 
d. A decisive rebalancing towards capital expenditure, particularly in technology 
upgradation, infrastructure creation and pro ductivity-linked support for 
MSMEs. 
e. The Ministry submit a concrete, time -bound roadmap for strengthening 
expenditure planning, internal financial controls and outcome-based monitoring. 
(Para-2.24) 
 
BUDGET ANNOUNCEMENTS 2026-27 
 
12. The Committee acknowledges that the Union Budget 2026 -27 has articulated a 
forward-looking framework for the MSME sector. However, the Committee notes with 
concern that several of the new announcements lack explicit budget -head mapping in 
the Expenditure Budget, raising questions ab out their implementability within the 
current fiscal year. (Para-2.26) 
 
13. Specifically: 
 
 The ₹10,000 crore SME Growth Fund is not explicitly shown in the Expenditure 
Budget. The Ministry has informed the Committee that "Preliminary 
deliberations are taking place for implementation of the Budget 
Announcements" and that "Post Budget webinars are being planned so that 
contours o f the initiative can be developed in consultation/ownership of all 
stakeholders". This is unsatisfactory — a Budget announcement of this 
magnitude requires immediate operationalisation with clear budget -head 
identification, annual release schedules, and implementation timelines. 
 The TReDS -GeM integration and CGTMSE guarantee for invoice discounting 
lack explicit IT infrastructure investment plans, implementation timelines, and 
fund sources. 

70 
 
 The Corporate Mitras programme has no clear funding mechanism, budg et 
allocation for FY 2026 -27, or cost -sharing arrangement among ICAI, ICSI and 
ICMAI. 
 The 200 legacy clusters announcement lacks a corresponding explicit budget line 
item. The Ministry has not clarified whether this will be funded under RAMP, 
MSE-CDP, SFURTI, or a new head. (Para-2.27) 
 
14. The Committee is constrained to observe that persistent reliance on procedural 
relaxations — continuously for two financial years — and end -year expenditure 
concentration has undermined the effective translation of budget announcements into 
tangible benefits for MSMEs.The Committee further strongly recommends that all new 
MSME-related budget announcements be supported by time -bound implementation 
frameworks, with quarterly physical and financial milestones aligned to the QEP and 
MEP. Announcements without demonstrable readiness in terms of guidelines, approvals 
and delivery mechanisms should not be rolled out, as repeated slippages weaken policy 
credibility and dilute intended outcomes for MSMEs.  (Para-2.28) 
OVERALL BUDGET ANALYSIS 2026-27 
15. The Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry, in consultation with the 
Ministry of Finance, seek necessary approval to redeploy unutilised or surrendered 
funds under GECL to other priority MSME schemes where funding requirements are 
acute. The Committee also emp hasises that since GECL allocations are booked under 
the MSME budget and were intended to support MSMEs under stress, their 
redeployment within the MSME ecosystem would remain fully aligned with the original 
policy objective. (Para-2.41) 
 
16. The Committee  also observes that guarantee -based schemes, particularly the 
Guaranteed Emergency Credit Line (GECL), account for a very large share of the 
Ministry‘s outlay, whereas allocations for technology centres, cluster infrastructure, 
skilling, green transition a nd market development remain relatively modest. 
Recognising the vital counter -cyclical role played by GECL and similar instruments 
during and after the pandemic, the Committee nevertheless recommends that, over the 
course of the next Finance Commission cyc le, the Ministry, in consultation with the 
Ministry of Finance, gradually rebalance its portfolio so that the share of pure 
guarantee-style interventions is reduced relative to deeper, capacity -building 
investments in productivity, competitiveness and resilience of MSMEs. (Para-2.42) 
 
17. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry institute a mandatory 
mid-year expenditure review mechanism for all schemes that have witnessed a BE -to-
RE reduction exceeding 30% in any of the preceding three financial years. Such 
schemes — particularly SFURTI, TCSP and New TC/ECs — should be required to 
furnish scheme -specific implementation roadmaps with quarterly milestones, and 
Budget Estimates for subsequent years should be calibrated against demonstrated 

71 
 
absorptive capacity rather than aspirational targets. The Committee is of the view that 
credible budgeting, anchored in realistic assessment of implementation readiness, is a 
prerequisite for restoring parliamentary confidence in the Ministry's expenditure 
planning. (Para-2.43) 
PUBLIC PROCUREMENT POLICY FOR MSMEs 
18. In the light of the information gathered by the Committee, it strongly 
recommends that the Ministry, in coordination with the Department of Public 
Enterprises and procuring CPSEs, put in place a time-bound and enforceable 
mechanism to achieve the mandated sub -targets for SC/ST -owned and women -owned 
MSEs. This should include CPSE -wise annual sub -targets, mandatory disclosure of 
shortfalls with reasons, and strengthening of MoU -linked penalties so t hat non -
compliance results in tangible managerial consequences rather than mere mark 
deductions. The Committee further recommends targeted vendor development drives 
exclusively for SC/ST and women -owned MSEs in technical and high -value sectors, 
with mandat ory handholding for GeM onboarding and tender participation, and 
institutionalised post-VDP mentoring with structured vendor -to-buyer matching. Time-
bound integration of the MSME Sambandh Portal with GeM and creation of a 
centralised national vendor direct ory should be completed within a defined timeline to 
enable real-time accountability and evidence-based procurement planning. (Para-2.49) 
19. The Committee notes the Ministry‘s submission that there is presently no 
provision for monitoring procurement from  MSEs owned by Other Backward Classes 
(OBCs) on the MSME Sambandh portal and that introducing an additional sub -target 
category may increase compliance burden and create overlaps with existing SC/ST and 
women sub-targets. The Committee, while conscious of these constraints, recommends 
that the Government examine the legal and administrative feasibility of tracking, and 
where appropriate incentivising, procurement from OBC -owned MSEs, without 
diluting the focus on achieving the existing sub -targets for SC/ST - and women-owned 
MSEs. (Para-2.50) 
DELAYED  PAYMENTS: A STRUCTURAL CHALLENGE 
20. Therefore, the Committee recommends that the Ministry strengthen the 
Samadhaan and ODR ecosystem through mandatory buyer compliance, integration 
with GeM for automatic flagging of delayed payments, and time -bound resolution 
mandates backed by penal provisions under the MSMED Act, 2006. (Para-2.53) 
QUALITY OF OUTPUT-OUTCOME FRAMEWORK AND DATA GOVERNANCE 
21. The Committee recommends that the Ministry undertake a comprehensive OOF 
redesign in consultation with NITI Aayog and CGA, ensuring SMART indicators with 
balanced output, outcome and impact metrics, clear baselines and verification 
protocols. All OOF data sho uld be subjected to annual third -party audits, and future 

72 
 
DFGs should include a performance scorecard highlighting schemes with consistent 
over/under-achievement and corrective actions taken. (Para-2.56) 
NITI AAYOG'S REPORT ON ENHANCING COMPETITIVENESS OF MSMES 
22. Taking the Report of NITI Aayog on ‗Enhancing MSMEs' Competitiveness in 
India‘ forward, the Committee recommends that the Ministry formally adopt a 
competitiveness framework aligned with NITI Aayog's recommendations, mapping 
each major scheme to the specific pillars of financing, skills, technology adoption and 
market access. In view of the structural ―missing middle‖, wherein medium enterprises 
account for only a small share of MSME units but contribute a disproportionately high 
share of MSME exp orts, a dedicated Medium Enterprise Window within RAMP and 
the SRI Fund should be designed and operationalised for Industry 4.0 adoption, R&D 
collaboration and deeper integration into global value chains. Cluster -based testing and 
certification facilities under MSE-CDP and Technology Centres should be accelerated 
through a time -bound action plan, prioritising sectors and clusters with high export 
potential identified in the NITI Aayog report. (Para-2.59) 
 
CHAPTER 3: SCHEME-WISE ANALYSIS 
GUARANTEED EMERGENCY CREDIT LINE (GECL) 
23. Considering a scenario as discussed above, the Committee is of the firm view that 
unutilised guarantee allocations should not be surrendered mechanically. Instead, given 
that these funds are already reflected under the MSME head, the Committee strongly 
recommends that the Ministry pursue the matter with the Ministry of Finance to retain 
and repurpose the available fiscal space for MSME priorities. (Para-3.4) 
 
24. The Committee further recommends that such funds be strategically redeployed 
to strengthen credit support, skill development, technology upgradation and 
region‑specific interventions, particularly for the North‑Eastern Region, aspirational 
districts and other under‑serv ed areas, as well as for MSME schemes demonstrating 
higher absorption capacity and developmental impact. The Committee underscores that 
retaining this buffer is fiscally prudent, as it provides policy flexibility to respond swiftly 
to future unpredictable shocks, rather than re‑mobilising resources afresh at a later 
stage. (Para-3.5) 
 
CREDIT GUARANTEE SUPPORT: CGTMSE 
25. In view of the above, the Committee strongly recommends that the Ministry 
urgently shift the assessment of the Credit Guarantee Scheme from a mere approval‑ 
and disbursement‑driven framework to a results‑ and impact‑b ased monitoring system. 
The Ministry should mandatorily track and place before the Committee 
beneficiary‑level outcomes, including enterprise survival beyond one and three years, 
employment generated or sustained, turnover growth, repayment and NPA trends,  and 

73 
 
graduation of units from micro to small categories, with disaggregation by social 
category and region. (Para-3.10) 
 
26. The Committee further recommends strict enforcement of collateral‑free lending 
norms under CGTMSE. Banks must not dilute the intent  of the scheme by demanding 
collateral or third‑party guarantees. Any deviation from scheme guidelines should 
require mandatory written justification, and repeated violations at the branch level 
should attract deterrent penalties. The Committee also recomm ends rationalisation of 
guarantee fees, bank charges and insurance practices, including limiting insurance 
coverage strictly to the outstanding loan balance, in order to reduce the effective cost of 
borrowing for micro and small enterprises. (Para-3.11) 
 
27. The Committee also recommends comprehensive reform of credit appraisal 
practices under CGTMSE. Excessive reliance on CIBIL scores should be curtailed, 
particularly for first‑generation entrepreneurs and youth, and alternative assessment 
parameters based on business viability, cash flow and local economic conditions should 
be institutionalised. To address persistent awareness gaps, the Committee recommends 
mandatory outreach targets for banks in rural and semi‑urban areas, supported by 
structured handhold ing through MSME Development Institutes and State‑level 
agencies. (Para-3.12) 
 
28. The Committee further recommends strengthening transparency, monitoring 
and institutional coordination. A comprehensive public dashboard for CGTMSE should 
be created, providing scheme‑wise data on applications, sanctions, rejections, sectoral 
coverage and employment outcomes. Successful State‑level MSME convergence models 
should be replicated nationwide, and structured coordination among Central 
Ministries, State Governments, banks and MSME support institutions should be 
institutionalised to ensure uniform imp lementation and long‑term resilience of the 
MSME credit ecosystem. (Para-3.13) 
PRIME MINISTER‘S EMPLOYMENT GENERATION PROGRAMME (PMEGP) 
29. In light of the above, the Committee recommends expeditious rollout of the 
PMEGP 2.0 single‑window portal within a defined timeline, followed by outcome‑based 
monitoring of key indicators such as application‑to‑disbursement time, 
grievance‑redressal timelines and bank/State‑wise performance. Periodic analytical 
reports should be placed before the Committee to ensure im proved efficiency, 
transparency and accountability. (Para-3.17) 
 
30. The Committee is also of the concerted view that the low uptake and lower 
sanction rates of offline applications reflect inadequate awareness, insufficient 
handholding by implementing agencies and weak facilitation at the grassroots level. The 
Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry devise a targeted outreach and 
capacity‑building strategy for offline applicants, particularly in rural areas, aspirational 

74 
 
districts and among women,  SC and ST beneficiaries, including mandatory facilitation 
counters at KVIC/KVIB/DIC offices, involvement of CSCs, SHGs and NGOs as 
application‑support partners, periodic awareness drives in local languages and 
structured training of field officials to ens ure parity in appraisal quality and sanction 
outcomes between offline and online applications. (Para-3.18) 
 
31. The Committee, in view of these structural and implementation deficiencies, 
recommends a comprehensive recalibration of PMEGP to restore its relevance, 
inclusiveness and employment‑generating potential. The Committee strongly 
recommends that the Ministry revi se the project‑cost ceiling for manufacturing units 
upward from the existing ₹50 lakh, with periodic indexation to inflation, and expand 
eligibility beyond proprietary enterprises to include partnerships and other suitable 
business forms, so as to enable s cale, formalisation and higher‑quality employment.  
(Para-3.21) 
 
32. The Committee further recommends time‑bound and accountable release of 
margin‑money subsidy, with clearly prescribed stage‑wise timelines, automatic 
escalation in cases of delay and robust  offline fallback mechanisms to address portal 
downtime, particularly in rural, hilly and North‑Eastern regions. To address 
persistently high bank rejection rates, the Committee urges the Ministry to issue 
binding advisories to banks for uniform applicatio n of collateral‑free norms, moderated 
use of CIBIL scores for first‑generation entrepreneurs and introduction of risk‑sharing 
or partial credit‑guarantee mechanisms to realign lending behaviour with the scheme‘s 
social objectives. (Para-3.22) 
 
33. The Comm ittee also recommends revamping Entrepreneurship Development 
Programmes by restoring adequate duration, strengthening physical training 
components and linking EDP completion with structured post‑sanction handholding, 
mentoring and market‑linkage support. I n parallel, the Committee calls for urgent 
augmentation of manpower and field capacity in KVIC, DICs and implementing offices 
to ensure effective outreach, appraisal and monitoring. Finally, the Committee 
recommends that the Ministry adopt a region‑ and se ctor‑specific facilitation approach, 
with dedicated support for high‑potential activities such as oil and gas services in Assam 
and agarwood‑based enterprises in the North‑East, through coordinated policy backing, 
technical assistance and market linkage, t o maximise PMEGP‘s developmental impact.  
(Para-3.23) 
 
34. Further, in view of high demand, strong historical utilisation (around 98 per cent 
of the approved outlay under the current EFC cycle in the case of PMEGP) and the 
critical role of these schemes in supporting first -generation and vulnerable 
entrepreneurs, the Committee recommends that, subject to the overall fiscal 
consolidation path and resource availability, the Government consider higher 
allocations for PMEGP and PM Vishwakarma in forthcoming Budget exercises. Within 
the envelope approved, the Committee further urges the Ministry to give clear 

75 
 
operational priority to women, SC/ST and aspirational -district beneficiaries by 
tightening monitoring and handholding mechanisms. (Para-3.24) 
PM VISHWAKARMA SCHEME 
35. The Committee accordingly, recommends that the Government undertake an 
immediate structural rationalisation of the PM Vishwakarma Scheme by addressing 
systemic bottlenecks across the beneficiary pipeline. This should include strict 
time‑binding and simplification of Gram Panchayat and Urban Local Body verification 
through automated escalation and independent audits, transparent communication 
regarding the registration cap and pending applications and strengthened district‑level 
oversight to eliminate delays, subjectivity and beneficiary uncertainty. (Para-3.30) 
 
36. The Committee further recommends that the scheme be reoriented from a static, 
trade‑bound framework to a dynamic, market‑responsive livelihood programme. This 
would require periodic expansion and up dating of the eligible trade list, flexibility for 
beneficiaries to switch or upgrade trades, modernisation of training curricula with 
active industry participation and strengthening of the Guru –Shishya model through 
improved incentives to ensure relevance , quality and continuity of skill development.  
(Para-3.31) 
 
37. The Committee also recommends a decisive shift from input‑driven 
implementation to outcome‑based delivery. This should include strengthening credit 
linkage through greater branch‑level account ability and more flexible norms for 
first‑time and small‑ticket borrowers, enhanced beneficiary awareness on loan terms 
and the introduction of robust outcome indicators such as post‑training income 
enhancement, productivity gains, enterprise sustainabilit y and market access, to ensure 
that scheme interventions translate into durable and measurable livelihood 
improvements. (Para-3.32) 
 
38. The Committee further notes that the Budget Estimate for the PM Vishwakarma 
Scheme has been reduced to ₹3,860.89 crore in FY 2026‑27 from ₹5,100 crore in FY 
2025‑26 despite full utilisation of the registration cap and pending liabilities towards 
training, toolkit delivery and interest subvention.This budget compression, despite high 
demand and pending liabilities, warrants  urgent review of allocation adequacy in light 
of scheme scale and first-generation entrepreneur support. (Para-3.33) 
39. In addition, the Committee notes heavy trade‑wise concentration in occupations 
whose nomenclature is commonly perceived as caste‑linked in several regions, and finds 
that this undermines the inclusiveness and pan‑India acceptability of the scheme. (Para-
3.34) 
 
40. The Committee therefore recommends that the Ministry urgently rationalise 
trade nomenclature under the PM Vishwakarma Scheme by replacing caste‑ or 
region‑associated terms with profession‑neutral, function‑based names (for example, 

76 
 
―Footwear Artisan‖ instead of ―Cobbler‖, ―Ceramic and Clay Product Maker‖ instead 
of ―Potter‖ and ―Personal Grooming Service Provider‖ instead of ―Barber‖), in 
consultation with States and social experts, and notify a revised, standardised trade list 
applicable uniformly across the country. (Para-3.35) 
INFRASTRUCTURE DEVELOPMENT: RAMP, MSE‑CDP, NEW TECHNOLOGY 
CENTRES AND TCSP 
41. The Committee accordingly recommends that the Ministry further sharpen the 
results‑based financing framework under RAMP by sequencing annual budgetary 
allocations strictly against the maturity of State‑level reforms and readiness of 
approved projects under Strategic Investment Plans. The Committee also recommends 
closer handholding of States with weaker institutional capaci ty to accelerate milestone 
achievement so that the remaining period of the programme is utilised to consolidate 
reforms on credit flow, market access, green transition and delayed payments and 
ensure full and timely utilisation of the approved outlay. (Para-3.39) 
 
42. In view of the above, the Committee recommends that the Ministry recalibrate 
conscious annual budgetary allocations under MSE‑CDP on the basis of committed 
liabilities and project‑wise implementation readiness, rather than uniform year‑on‑ year 
allocations. The Committee also recommends stricter milestone‑linked fund release 
mechanisms, improved handholding of State Governments and SPVs in project 
execution and time‑bound completion of CFCs and industrial‑estate projects to prevent 
cost over runs and idle infrastructure. Given the scheme‘s higher assistance for NER, 
aspirational districts, LWE‑affected areas and clusters dominated by micro, women and 
SC/ST‑owned units, the Committee recommends that such priority clusters be accorded 
first charge on available funds so that the equity and regional development objectives of 
the scheme are fully realised. (Para-3.43) 
 
43. The Committee recommends that the Ministry institutionalise a pre‑commitment 
framework under which approvals and budget provisio ning for new Technology 
Centres and Extension Centres are linked to upfront, time‑bound commitments from 
State Governments for land and built‑up space. The Committee further recommends 
prioritisation of funds for locations where land is already in possession and tenders have 
been finalised under the Autonomous/EPC mode, and early operationalisation of 
additional Extension Centres in aspirational districts and the NER, supported by 
PMIS‑based monitoring, so that revised allocations translate into tangible tr aining and 
technology services for MSMEs rather than recurring under‑expenditure. (Para-3.47) 
44. In this context, The  Committee recommends that the Ministry adopt a holistic 
phase‑wise, completion‑linked planning and budgeting approach for TCSP, aligning 
annual physical targets and financial allocations strictly with the commissioning status 
of individual centres and rea diness of procurement packages. The Committee also 
recommends tighter contractual safeguards and performance‑based monitoring of 
contractors and procurement agencies, alongside enhanced coordination with CPWD 

77 
 
and State authorities, to avoid time and cost o verruns. Given the strong outcomes 
already delivered by operational centres, the Committee recommends prioritising 
completion and full operationalisation of the remaining Technology Centres before 
expanding targets so that the proposed allocation for FY 20 26‑27 results in optimal 
utilisation of funds and durable strengthening of MSME competitiveness. (Para-3.50) 
EQUITY, ENTREPRENEURSHIP AND TRAINING 
45. The Committee appreciates the commitment shown by the Ministry to support 
MSMEs and recommends that the enhanced allocation under the SRI Fund be deployed 
in a targeted, outcome‑oriented manner, prioritising MSMEs with high growth and 
export potential and those affected by external trade disruptions, with a focus on 
technology upgradation, product diversifica tion and quality certification. The 
Committee further recommends strengthening the pipeline of investible MSMEs from 
Tier‑II and Tier‑III regions through structured handholding, incubation support and 
convergence with other MSME schemes, and instituting a robust monitoring 
framework with measurable indicators such as enterprise scale expansion, employment 
generation, export growth and private‑capital mobilisation to guide future allocations 
under the Fund. (Para-3.52) 
 
46. As it acknowledges the enhanced allocation for ATI, the Committee recommends 
that the enhanced allocation for ATI be utilised in a timely and optimal manner by 
aligning training and institutional‑support activities with emerging industry 
requirements, export‑market standards and technology‑upgradation needs of MSMEs. 
The Committee further recommends strengthening partnerships between training 
institutions, industry bodies, exporters and technology providers so that trainees 
acquire upskilling, market‑relevant  competencies, and instituting an outcome‑tracking 
framework covering enterprise creation, employment generation, export‑readiness and  
technology adoption to maximise the impact of this investment. (Para-3.54) 
KHADI, VILLAGE INDUSTRIES, COIR AND MARKET PROMOTION – KEY 
ISSUES 
47. The Committee therefore recommends just rationalization of establishment 
expenditure under Khadi Grant and systematic redirection of savings to field -level 
interventions that directly benefit artisans and rural enterprises. The Committee also 
recommends linking support such as Modified Market Development Assistance and 
marketing‑infrastructure assistance to measurable improvements in sales turnover, 
artisan incomes and institutional viability, so that financial assistance leads t o sustained 
competitiveness rather than continued reliance on subsidies. (Para-3.56) 
 
48.     The Committee notes that the Ministry has drawn up a milestone -based quarterly 
plan (20 –30–30–20) for utilisation of the ₹196 crore allocation  in 2026 –27. The 
Committee recommends that the Ministry strictly adhere to its own milestone -linked 
phasing, with particular focus on expediting civil works, machinery installation and 

78 
 
commissioning, so that all sanctioned clusters reach functional status by the end of FY 
2026–27. The Committee further recommends that the Ministry furnish to it, by a 
specified date, a detailed status note on cluster -wise physical progress, fund releases and 
bottlenecks, along with corrective measures taken. (Para-3.58) 
 
49.     The Committee fails to comprehend the delays which it is of the firm believe 
should have been circumvented and recommends strict adherence to the 
milestone-linked plan for settlement of committed liabilities under SFURTI, with 
priority accorded to fun ctionalisation and operational readiness of clusters rather than 
mere financial closure. The Committee further recommends fixing accountability on 
Nodal and Implementing Agencies for avoidable delays in procurement and clearances, 
and systematic incorporat ion of lessons learnt from SFURTI into the design and 
execution of future cluster -based schemes such as MSE -CDP, particularly for 
traditional and artisan-based industries. (Para-3.59) 
 
50. The Committee expresses disappointment on the neglect to indigenous  section 
such as Coir and recommends that the Coir Board improve utilisation of funds through 
advance planning and timely execution of activities, expand outreach in non‑traditional 
coir‑producing States to achieve more balanced regional coverage and accel erate 
commercial‑scale adoption of research outputs through structured industry linkages 
and incubation support, so that S&T investments yield tangible gains in productivity, 
diversification and incomes for coir workers and entrepreneurs. (Para-3.61) 
 
51. The Committee recommends that PMS and IC be deployed more strategically as 
market-promotion and resilience instruments by adopting a flexible, shock -responsive 
funding approach—especially during periods of global trade stress—and by redesigning 
these schem es with clear, outcome -linked objectives related to export diversification, 
domestic-market substitution and sustained buyer linkages. The Committee further 
recommends closer integration of PMS and IC activities into a unified market -resilience 
framework s o that MSMEs receive coordinated support across domestic and 
international markets in response to evolving global trade uncertainties. (Para-3.64) 
 
CHAPTER 4: TARGETED SCHEMES / PROGRAMMES FOR VULNERABLE 
GROUPS 
NORTH EAST REGION 
52. In view of the persistent under -utilisation of funds despite adequate allocations, 
the Committee recommends that the Ministry put in place a mandatory time -bound 
execution framework for all NER projects, with clearly defined quarterly physical and 
financial milestones and release of funds strictly linked to their achievement. The 
Ministry should also conduct quarterly project -wise reviews and ensure reallocation of 
funds from delayed or non -performing projects to ready -to-execute projects within the 

79 
 
same financial year, so that enhanced allocations result in actual expenditure and visible 
outcomes in the NER. (Para-4.7) 
 
53. The Committee notes wide inter -State variation in PMEGP -supported micro 
enterprises across the North Eastern States. While Assam continues to account for the 
highest number of assisted units, several States such as Manipur, Mizoram, Meghalaya 
and Sikkim show fluctuating or declining trends in recent years, particularly in 2022 -23 
and 2023 -24, with partial recovery in 2024 -25. The Co mmittee is of the view that the 
uneven distribution of benefits, coupled with declining expenditure utilisation, suggests 
that existing institutional and delivery mechanisms require closer monitoring and more 
focused implementation to ensure that allocated  resources translate into actual project 
grounding and enterprise creation across all North Eastern States in an equitable and 
timely manner.  (Para-4.11) 
 
54. In view of the wide inter -State variation in PMEGP performance in the North 
Eastern Region, the Committee recommends that the Ministry fix State -wise PMEGP 
targets linked to past performance and absorptive capacity, provide focused 
handholding through KVIC/KVIB and District Industries Centres in consistently low -
performing States, and conduct quarter ly State -specific reviews to ensure timely 
grounding of projects and equitable distribution of benefits across all North Eastern 
States.  (Para-4.12) 
 
WOMEN 
 
55. The Committee therefore, recommends that the Ministry consider earmarking a 
minimum assured allocation for women entrepreneurs under PMEGP to safeguard 
their participation during periods of budgetary constraint. It further recommends that 
the Ministry explore  differential or graded subsidy support for women -led micro 
enterprises, especially in low-capital and service sectors, to mitigate the impact of rising 
project costs. The Committee also suggests strengthening convergence with skill 
development, market lin kage and mentoring initiatives to enhance the viability of 
women-led units, and instituting periodic monitoring of gender -disaggregated outcomes 
to ensure that the objective of inclusive and equitable entrepreneurship promotion 
under PMEGP is consistently achieved.  (Para-4.17) 
 
SCHEDULED CASTES/ SCHEDULED TRIBES 
 
56. The Committee recommends that the Ministry reassess the budgetary allocation 
for NSSH in light of the demonstrated demand and the strategic importance of inclusive 
entrepreneurship in the MSME ecosystem. Adequate and stable funding should be 
ensured to strengthen credit facilitation, procurement readiness and enterprise capacity 
building, particularly to accelerate progress towards the 4% procurement mandate. 
The Ministry should also improve fund utilisation efficiency through better planning, 

80 
 
monitoring an d convergence with other MSME schemes to maximise the impact of 
available resources.  (Para-4.22) 
 
SPECIALLY – ABLED PERSONS 
 
57. The Committee observes that despite preferential provisions, the number of 
beneficiaries has shown a consistent decline over the last five years, falling from 484 in 
2021-22 to 213 in 2024 -25 and further to 199 in the current year up to 31 December 
2025. This  downward trend suggests gaps in outreach, accessibility and effective 
utilisation of the scheme by differently-abled entrepreneurs. (Para-4.25) 
58. The Committee recommends that the Ministry earmark a minimum annual sub -
target under PMEGP exclusively for differently-abled beneficiaries, ensure district-wise 
identification of eligible cases through District Industries Centres, provide structured 
handholding support by KVIC/KVIB officials from application filing to loan 
disbursement, and undertake quarterly reviews of performance indicating applications 
mobilised, sanctioned and units operationalised for differently -abled persons.  (Para-
4.26) 
CHAPTER 5: AUTONOMOUS BODIES 
KHADI AND VILLAGE INDUSTRIES COMMISSION (KVIC) 
 
59. Therefore, the Committee recommends that KVIC formulate a comprehensive 
medium-term strategy to substantially expand artisan coverage and employment 
generation, with clearly defined annual physical and financial targets. 
Capacity-building initiatives under CoEK should be significantly scaled  up in coverage 
and geographical outreach, with measurable outcome indicators linked to productivity, 
quality improvement and income enhancement. KVIC should also strengthen 
institutional capacity by ensuring availability of adequate technical expertise an d 
reducing excessive reliance on short -term contractual arrangements. Focused efforts 
are further recommended to enhance branding, product diversification, e -commerce 
integration and export promotion. (Para-5.10) 
 
COIR BOARD 
 
60. The Committee therefore, r ecommends that the Ministry strengthen value 
addition, product diversification, and branding to improve export realisation. Skill 
development and technology transfer initiatives should be substantially scaled up with 
measurable outcomes linked to productiv ity and artisan incomes, particularly for 
women workers. The Ministry should also ensure timely release and efficient utilisation 
of funds to support effective implementation of programmes and sustained sectoral 
growth. (Para-5.18) 
 

81 
 
61. The Committee there fore, recommends that the Ministry formulate a targeted 
export resilience strategy for the coir sector, including market diversification beyond 
traditional destinations, support for compliance with international standards, and 
financial risk -mitigation mea sures for MSME exporters. The Ministry may also 
coordinate with the Ministry of Commerce to proactively address tariff -related 
challenges through trade negotiations and export incentive frameworks. (Para-5.20) 
NATIONAL SMALL INDUSTRIES CORPORATION (NSIC) 
62.     The Committee notes that NSIC has demonstrated strong institutional capacity 
and operational performance through its nationwide network, integrated service 
delivery model and consistent financial results. However, the Committee is of the 
considered view that the scale of financing and growth capital required by the MSME 
sector—particularly for first -generation entrepreneurs, technology -intensive 
enterprises, export-oriented units and enterprises located in aspirational or underserved 
regions—far exce eds the present resource envelope available with NSIC. The 
Committee observes that the absence of a dedicated, large -scale growth financing 
mechanism significantly constrains the Corporation‘s ability to catalyse private 
investment and support MSMEs in sca ling up operations, thereby limiting its potential 
developmental impact. (Para-5.25) 
 
63. The Committee, therefore, strongly recommends that the Ministry of MSME, in 
consultation with the Ministry of Finance, operationalise the proposed ₹10,000 crore 
SME Growth Fund under NSIC in a phased, multi‑year manner, with a clearly defined 
implementation framework, timelines and measurable outcome parameters. The 
Committee emphasises that the proposed Growth Fund should be structured as a 
professionally managed veh icle, distinct from existing credit and guarantee schemes, 
and should focus on providing growth‑stage financing through blended‑finance, 
risk‑sharing and co‑lending models in partnership with financial institutions. Priority 
should be accorded to MSMEs eng aged in technology upgradation, export‑oriented 
activities and enterprises operating in underserved and aspirational regions. (Para-5.26) 
 
64.     The Committee further recommends that robust governance mechanisms be 
institutionalised for the proposed Grow th Fund, including the establishment of an 
independent investment committee, transparent eligibility criteria, periodic public 
disclosure of fund utilisation and outcome‑based monitoring linked to employment 
generation, enterprise growth and market access.  A mid‑term evaluation framework 
should also be incorporated to enable timely course correction and ensure that the Fund 
contributes meaningfully to scaling MSME competitiveness and long‑term 
sustainability, while remaining consistent with the overall fisc al consolidation path.  
(Para-5.27) 
 
65.     The Committee also observes that despite NSIC‘s expanded mandate, upgraded 
Schedule ‗A‘ status and commendable financial performance, its existing equity base of 

82 
 
approximately ₹532 crore remains modest relative t o the scale of operations and 
financial support expected from the Corporation. The Committee notes that this limited 
capital base constrains NSIC‘s leverage capacity and necessitates greater reliance on 
borrowings from banks and financial institutions, oft en at higher costs, which 
ultimately affects the affordability of assistance extended to MSMEs. (Para-5.28) 
 
66.     Accordingly, the Committee recommends that the Ministry consider substantial 
equity infusion into NSIC  at the earliest to strengthen its capital base in line with its 
strategic importance and enhanced responsibilities. The Committee is of the view that 
enhanced equity support would reduce dependence on high -cost borrowings, improve 
internal resource generation, and enable NSIC to offer more competitive interest rates, 
lower service charges and affordable support to MSMEs. (Para-5.29) 
 
67.     The Committee further recommends that any equity infusion into NSIC be 
explicitly linked to measurable expansion in MSME coverage, particularly in priority 
sectors and underserved regions, so that the intervention directly translates into lower 
cost of finance, improved credit accessibility and sustainable scaling of NSIC 
operations, in alignment with national objective s such as Atmanirbhar Bharat and 
Viksit Bharat. (Para-5.30) 
MAHATMA GANDHI INSTITUTE FOR RURAL INDUSTRIALISATION (MGIRI) 
68. In view of the enhanced financial support and MGIRI‘s expanding portfolio of 
technology development, quality assurance and capacity-building activities, the 
Committee recommends that the Ministry put in place a clearly articulated medium -
term outcomes framework for MGIRI, with defined milestones for technology 
dissemination, field -level adoption by Khadi and Village Industries , and measurable 
improvements in artisan incomes and rural enterprise productivity. The Committee 
further emphasises that future budgetary support should be closely aligned with 
MGIRI‘s role as a national resource centre, ensuring that increased allocation s 
translate into scalable, replicable and impact-oriented interventions across States. (Para-
5.33)

9. The Chairman welcomed the Secretary and Officers of the Ministry of MSME and its 
allied agencies to the meeting to discuss the Ministry‘s budgetary allocations for FY 2026-27. 
In his introductory remarks, the Chairman: 
 
(i) Acknowledged the budgetary allocation made to the Ministry for 2026–27; 
(ii) Sought clarification on the gap between projected demand and actual allocation 
(iii) Expressed concern over the relatively low proportion of capital expenditure; 
(iv) Emphasized on revising the definition of MSMEs and consider creating a lower 
category (e.g., nano enterprises) to better support very small units;  
Asked about employment generation targets and technological upgra dation 
measures; 
(v) Sought data on MSME closures and sector-wise NPAs; 
(vi) Raised concerns regarding awareness and accessibility of digital platforms and 
schemes. 
 
10. After the Chair‘s permission, the Secretary, M/o MSME apprised the Committee on 
the 2026-27 budget highlights, including: 
 
(i) Key budgetary highlights and major policy initiatives introduced to strengthen the 
MSME ecosystem, with particular emphasis on enhancing competitiveness, 
technology adoption and market integration. 

86 
 
(ii) Measures undertaken to facilit ate access to credit, including expansion of credit 
guarantee schemes, interest subvention support and development of customised 
financial products tailored to the needs of micro and small enterprises. 
(iii) Priority sectoral interventions focusing on industries  such as footwear, leather, 
toys, clean technology and startups, aimed at promoting innovation, employment 
generation and export potential. 
(iv) Implementation of Public Procurement Policy provisions, including targeted 
support and capacity -building measures fo r SC/ST and women entrepreneurs to 
improve their participation in government procurement. 
(v) Steps taken to promote formalisation of enterprises, bridge existing credit gaps 
and enhance domestic and global market access through digital platforms, cluster 
development and institutional support mechanisms. 
11. The Chairman and Members of the Committee raised a wide range of issues, inter 
alia, the following: 
(i) Absence of clear implementation roadmaps, timelines and accountability 
mechanisms for major Budget announcements such as the SME Growth Fund, 
TReDS integration and Corporate Mitra programme; 
(ii) Disproportionate emphasis on equity financing vis -à-vis skill development and 
entrepreneurship promotion; 
(iii) Pendency, verification delays and rejection trends under P M Vishwakarma 
Yojana, and assessment of income enhancement of beneficiaries; 
(iv) Need for collateral-free, cash-flow-based lending and concerns regarding ground -

Budget Estimates compared to last year budget estimates of 32 crores. Rs. 32.5 crores 
sought for in this current year Budget Estimates is to be spent for meeting expenses on two 
items, i.e., transport subsidy and establishment of Growth Centres. From the funds asked 
for under the Scheme, the Committee notes that adequate planning has not been done. The 
implementation is tardy. The backward areas in the country are in difficult terrain and Jack 
of basic infra!'.tructure. Concrete steps have, therefore. to be taken to motivate people to 

avail of the facilities and concessions under the Scheme. State Governments sometimes do 
not keep any provision for the purpose. The infrastructural deVelopment in the area for the 
establishment of Growth Centres is done by the Central Government only when the 
concerned State Government is ready to provide with the required funds. The entrepreneurs 
are caught in the cobweb of Central Government grant, State Government grant, loans from 
financial institutions and market borrowings. The entrepreneur finds extremely difficult and 
feels demotivated when he faces diffculties right from the acquisition of land, power supply, 
availability of water, etc. Many entrepreneurs have left midway their projects due to these 
factors and non-cooperation from different sections of Governmental machinery . The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that for the development of Growth Centres in the 
backward areas 'single window scheme' may be adopted as one of the motivating factors to 
willing entrepreneurs to establish industrial units in backward areas. The Committee would 
further recommend perfect coordination among the Central Government, concerned State 
Government and the financial institution· to make the Scheme successful. The Committee

tion has been approved in Industrial Sector relating to even Food Processing Industries to 
the tune of 8472.2 millions of rupees without any consideration for the growth of indigenous 
industries in this Sector. Food Processing Industry have to a large extent depend on the local 
ancillary small scale and village and cottage industries and thereby there is no safeguard for 
the survival and development of such industries. The Committee, therefore, recommends 
that :-
fa) disinvestment by PSUs and the funds accrued on account of the disinvestment 
should be utilised for reviving, and restructuring of the sick PSUs. The demand for 
grants and performance budget are totally silent on this aspect; 
(b) foreign investments should be approved in areas where we are yet to develop the 
technical know-how and depend upon foreign technology, The Government should 
ensure that foreign investment is earmarked for industries in the export sector to 
boost up the export of our industrial production. It should not disturb and dislocate 
the existing industrial growth of the country in the long run. The foreign 
collaboration should be identified for industries where we are lagging behind in 
international market. The Committee regrets to note that the demand for grants for 
the Department of Heavy Largest Industry does not perceive this situation and no 
funds have been allocated to organise and regulate foreign investment in our 
industrial sector particularly in the PSUs which we have developed and grown over 
a period of several decades but for which the present infrastructure for further 
development could not have been there; 
(c) every effort should be made to ensure that all the eight· benches of Board for 
Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) are made functional and the cases of 
sick PSUs pending before them are disposed off expeditiously to minimise the drain 
on the public funds. The Demands for Grants of the Department and the 
Performance Budget do not reflect any concern on the depleted strength of the 
BIFR benches and the expenditure and efforts to be made by the Department to 
make them functional;

The performance Budget of the Department is silent on the steps taken by it to check the 
downward graph. The Budget estimates for the year 1993-94 for this item is reduced to 40 
crores compared to 45 crores in the preceding year inspite of escalation in prices. 
This is a scheme to benefit educated unemployed youth with low income families and 30% 
of the beneficiaries are from SCJST categories. The Committee, therefore, recommends that 
the scheme should be implemented with all the available resources so as to ensure that the 
benefits envisaged under the scheme for self-employment provided to large number of 
persons and more funds are allocated. 
9. 7 (ii) Small Scale Industries: A sum of Rs .• 190.40 crores has been provided in the 
Budget Estimates for 1993-94. The revised estimates of 1992-93 were to the tune of Rs. 
147.41 crores. The Development of Small Scale Industries is organised through Development 
Commissioner of Small Scale Industries of the Department. The Committee finds that on 
administration and maintenance of the office of the Development Commissioner an amount 
of Rs. 3.68 crores is provided in the Budget Estimates with a component of 3.10 crores as 
non-plan expenditure. Rs. 58 lakhs are only for plan expenditure on two items i.e. publicity 
for 40 lakhs and for modernisation of library for 18 lakhs in the Budget Estimates. 
Comparing the budget figures for an important item like training which is 3.41 crores with 
that of the expenditure on the maintenance of the office of Development Commissioner, it 
may be seen that expenditure priorities are not on sound lines. The Committee, therefore, 
recommends that every step should be taken to regulate the expenditure on this item and 
the money thus saved may be earmarked for other developmental item(s) of the Small Scale 
Industries. 
9. 7 (iii) Khadi and Village Industries: Khadi and Village Industries have been earmarked a 
sum of Rs. 525.64 crores in the current year Budget Estimates compared to 352 crores in the 
last years revised estimates. The Khadi and Village Industries cover a vast majority of our 
population in different areas of the country and primarily cater to the needs of our 
economically weaker sections. The Khadi and Village Industries generate vast potential for 
local employment and if given correct direction and infrastructural support, Kha.di and 
Village Industries can be more helpful in our rural economy. The Committee, however, 
finds that inspite of budgetary support, Khadi and Village Industries have not been able to 
compete in the open market and stand on their legs. The reasons , therefore, have to be 
studied and perceptive planning is to be made to make a beginning so that Khadi and 
Village Industries become self-sufficient in their functioning in all respects. The Commit tee 
finds that no thought is given in the Demands for Grants and there is no expenditure on this 
account. The Committee therefore , recommends that the priorities of expenditure may be 

re-fixed and monetary allocation be made. The Committee further recommends that every 
effort should be made to ensure that Khadi and Village Industri es do not suffer from 
shortage of financial resources, lack of infrastructural support and bureaucratic red-tapi sm. It 
is essent ial that the problem of marketing of the finished goods is taken on top priority. The 
Government should issue instructions at least to their Departments that Khadi/Village/Small 
Scale Industries Products are purchased for their requirements on the pattern of encourage­
ment given for Handloom cloth. The other point the Committee emphasises that it should be 
made obligatory on the part of the establishments of such industrie s to pay minimum living 
wages to the employees. The Committee further recommends that concrete steps are to be 
taken to ensure for the general health and welfare of the workers. Co-operatives in the field 
are to be activised and finished goods are marketed for adequate return. The Committee is 
aware of the fact that rural masses are not gainfully employed throughout the year. Some 
programmes for motivating the rural masses to utilise their spare time in engaging 
themselves in such industries are to be devised. The Committee finds that though a sum of 
Rs. 525.54 crores has been earmarked in the Budget Estimates for this item yet no money 
has been allotted for motivating people and for awareness programm es on the role and the 
utility of Khadi and Village Industries to rural masses. The programme for training 
undertaken by the Department also lacks perception. The Committee opines that prog­
ramme for training should be so designed and chalked out so as to give on the spot training 
and guidance by mobile training personnel in the first instance to familiarise the rural masses 
about various projects/schemes under Khadi and Village Industrie s. The initial phase may 
inrer-alia include ground level information about project, equipment, finance and marketing 
facilities for finished products. Once this phase of training is completed and the masses are 
motivated and assured of additional revenue to the person or to the family then additional 
training programmes as envisaged by the Department in the Budget Estimates would yield 
positive results. The Committee, therefore, recommends that the thrust of the training 
programme should be reoriented and grouped into two phases as mentioned above. 
The Committee trusts that its observations and recommendations will receive serious 
considerat ion for implementation.

6. Taken into account the documents and other material made available to it and oral evidence tendered before 
it the Committee concludes as under :-
6.01 The Performance Budget of the Ministry of Mines for the year 1994-95 states that the Ministry is 
primarily responsible for the regulation and development of the mineral sector including the mining and 
metallurgy of all non ferrous metals both in private and public sectors but excluding Natural Gas , Petroleum 
coal and Atomic minerals. Mmeral resources are national assets. Conservation and planned exploitation of 
minerals are therefore, of prime importance to the national economy. Besides providing the basic inputs to 
domestic industry the mineral sector accounts for sizeable exports and foreign exchange earni ngs. Having 
regard to the extent and variety of mineral resources in the country there is great potential for rapid growth 
of this sector. It is the onus of the. Ministry of the Mines to develop this sector with utmost care and caution 
to enable this sector to compete with the contemporary globalisation in the internatio nal area. But the 
Committee finds that the entire mines and minerals sector is in doldrums. Large number of mines have either 
closed or at the brink of closure. The situation is very alarming particularl y in the States of Bihar , Andhra 
Pradesh , Rajasthan, Goa, Orissa, Madhya Pradesh etc. where a good number of Mines have closed dov·m. 
There is no provision in the Demands for Grants of the Ministry for the revival of closed Mines in the 
country. The Committee has not been told of any kind of package prepared by the Ministry for the reopening 
of closed mines in the country and make them viable. Rather the Committee has been told that the minerals 
belong to the State Governments. The onus of re-opening of closed mines is therefore the responsibility of 
the States and Ministry has washed its hands off by pointing out the responsibihty on the States ignoring 
the loss being caused to the nation due to the closure of mines throughout the country. The States faced with 
acute resource constraints and are unable to divert their attention towards the closed· mines. The 
Committee, therefore, recommends that the Government must also pay attention towards the closed/ 
closing mines throughout the country and prepare a comprehensive package for their revival in 
consultation with the State Governments concerned. There must be a perfect co-ordi nation between 

2 
the Governme nt and the Gove rnm ent of the States in thi s •·egard . The Governm ent should constitut e 
a tea m of experts to find out the causes of closure of mines and suggest the ways for their revival within 
a t ime frame. 
6.02 The Committee finds that there is lack of coordination between the Government and the Government 
of the States as far as regulating of mining is concerned. Responding to a query about the foreign investment 
in the mineral sector after the enactment of the Mines and Minerals (Regulation and Development) 
Amendment Act, 1994 the Secretary of Ministry of Mines states that the minerals belong to the State 
Governmen ts. All applicat ions have to be submitted by entrepreneurs to the concerned State Governments 
and it is they who have to give the prospecting licence or the mining lease as the case may be. The 
Government did not have precise information whether any State Government had received any formal 
proposa l and whether any foreign party has applied for any prospecting licence. The Committee finds it not 
convincing. After opening the mineral sector of the country for foreign investment and participation in order 
to accelerating i nflow of domestic and foreign capita l into the mineral sector the Governme nt has left the 
matter entirely to the State Governments. On such a vital issue there should have been a perfect 
understanding and coordination between the Central and State Governments. The Committ ee, ther efor e, 
recommends· that Governm ent must keep a watch on every foreign investment propo sal in the miner al 
sector and advi se the c once rn ed State Government to make best u se of such a propo sal with out 
compr omising nationa l interest and prioritie s and maintain the closest coordin ation with the State 
Govern ment in thi s regar d. If there are stron g sentiment s expr essed by the State Gove rnmen t, as far 
as possib le such sentiments should be respecte d. It is import ant th at compensation money reac hes the 
peo ple allocated to Geological Survey of India (GSI) in Major Head 2853. GS I plays a dominant role for 
the gro\\th of the Mineral sector of the country. According to the Perforn1ance Budget (1994- 95) of the 
Ministry GSI is responsible for collection. collation and dissemination of geological data and providing 
basic geologic~ I information essential for the successful implementation of practically are the developmen­
tal programmes of the count!). The investigation carried out by GSI contribute directly to the discovery and 
evaluation of mineral resources ensuring thereby the continued and steady supply of vital ra\\ materials to 
the core industrial sector . The results of investigation aid in the better understanding of the cmstal 
framework and the geological process with bearing on development in other as vital sectors such as 
agriculture, land use management, irrigation and power development. utilisation of water resources. 
development of transport and communication, educat ion and scientific management of environment. Thus 
survey and mapping and mineral exploration are the most important functions ofGSI for Mineral sector 
and geological process having bearing on other important sectors oft he country but the committee finds that 
out of the total allocation ofRs. 125.74% crores in BE 1994-95 only a sum ofRs. 11.20 crorcs has been 
earmarked for survey and mapping and Rs. 12.90 for mineral exploration. Thus a total sum ofRs. 25.10 
crores will be spent on the vital functions of Survey and mapping and Mineral exploration whereas more 
than Rs. I 00 crores will be spent on other purposes mainly administration etc. The committee, therefore, 
recommends that additional funds be allocated for such primary functio ns as survey and mapping and 
Mineral exploration of the GSI. Such Su rveys and exp lorat ion should conform to a precise ly ind icated 
time frame so that a check would be possib le on tangible res ults achieved. The Committee appreciates 
the gesture of the Government in increasing the resource Budgetary allocation to GSI as per its 
recommendations made in its Thjrd Report on the Demands for Grants of the Ministl) ' of Mines ( 1993-94 ).

INTRODUCTION
I,  the Chairman of the Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee  on Industry,  having   been  
authorised  by the  Committee, hereby present this 100 th Report of  Sub-Committee-I for  Ministry of Steel and Mines (
of Department-related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry)  on  Performance Review  of  National Mineral
Development Corporation Limited (NMDC) which is under the administrative control of  Ministry of Steel .
2.The Committee on Industry constituted Sub-Committee-I for Ministry of Steel and Mines .  The Sub-Committee took
up the issue of Performance Review of National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC)). The Sub-
Committee visited Hyderabad  from 28th and 29th June , 2002 and interacted with the  management of National Mineral
Development Corporation Limited (NMDC). 
3.            The Report has been prepared on  the basis of   on the spot  study and  interaction with the    Secretary ,
Ministry of Steel and officials  of National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC). 
4          The Sub-Committee in its meeting held on 17th  December, 2002  considered and adopted  the  Report. 
5.         The Committee at its meeting held on 17th December,  2002 considered and adopted the Report.         
 
NEW DELH
December   17, 2002   
                                      
 DR. P.C. ALEXANDER
Chairman
Department -related Parliamentary Standing Committee on Industry
REPORT
 
National Mineral Development Corporation Limited (NMDC) , a Government of India Enterprise and  a “Mini
Ratna Category-I” Company was established  in the year 1958, in pursuance of Industrial Policy Resolution of 1956 to
promote and undertake development of minerals (other than coal, oil and atomic minerals) in Public Sector. NMDC is
the largest producer and exporter of iron ore in this Country. Its exports are around 7 million tonnes of iron ore per
annum (through Minerals & Metals Trading Corporation Ltd - canalising agency). It has also exported about 1.7 MT of

100th Report of Committee on Industry
